#2770. Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon

While investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut, a very different IPO is making waves in Europe: Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the operator of one of the world's most famous geothermal spas.

Blue Lagoon Corp. raised roughly 14.3 billion Icelandic kronur ($110 million) through the offering, valuing the Icelandic geothermal spa operator at about $787 million, according to the company's investor presentation.

The Blue Lagoon traces its origins to 1992, when Blue Lagoon Ltd. was founded to study the water in the Blue Lagoon, an open-air pool of warm, milky-blue water set in a black lava field in southwestern Iceland. It grew into a business spanning a spa, hotels and skincare made with ingredients from the lagoon.

Shares will trade under the ticker "BLUE" on one of Europe's smallest stock exchanges, Nasdaq Iceland Main Market, part of the Nasdaq Nordic group, which also operates exchanges in Sweden, Denmark and Finland.

"Wellness is the new luxury, and we know that the wellness economy is growing faster than the economy as a whole, so we have tailwind from that," CEO Sigríður Margrét Oddsdóttir told CNBC on Thursday.

"Now is the right time for us to list," she added. "We are a company that thinks long-term, we have a clear vision for the next decade, and being publicly listed gives investors the opportunity to participate in our journey."

The company's operations are centered on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, where, as well as the Blue Lagoon geothermal spa, it runs the Silica Hotel, the Retreat luxury hotel and spa, and the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant.

It also operates the Kerlingarfjöll Highland Base and Hrauneyjar properties in Iceland's highlands, and sells Blue Lagoon-branded skincare products internationally.

The 34-year-old company has averaged 11% annual revenue growth over the past decade, and next year is expected to be a record, with revenue growing by more than half, Oddsdóttir said.

The company plans to use the raised capital to fund expanding its existing properties, acquiring businesses, and developing new destinations.

In total, nearly 4,000 subscriptions were received in the initial public offering, worth about 15.3 billion kronur, about 7% more than the total size of the offering, the company said, citing strong demand from smaller investors, including retail investors.

Iceland's relatively small stock market had just 27 companies on its main exchange at the end of 2025, according to Nasdaq. The market is dominated by banks, seafood companies and other domestically focused firms.

The global wellness industry reached $7.5 trillion in 2025, up 8.9% from the previous year, according to the Global Wellness Institute. Spending on thermal and mineral springs grew 10.4% over the same period, with the institute forecasting annual growth of nearly 10% for the sector through 2030.

Tourism accounted for nearly 9% of Iceland's GDP in 2025, and is growing, according to Statistics Iceland. The country welcomed around 2.3 million international visitors that year, with the U.S. as its largest source market.

#2769. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2768. Zak Brown says McLaren will always respect staff who want to skip Middle East races

Formula 1 is pressing ahead with its season-ending swing through the Middle East, and McLaren is making clear that no member of its travelling workforce will be forced onto the plane.

Speaking during Thursday's FIA team representatives' press conference at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown was asked whether his team would match the stance taken by Mercedes boss Toto Wolff and Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur, both of whom confirmed they would respect any employee choosing not to travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi over regional security concerns.

"Yes, of course," Brown replied. "We're an employee-first organisation. And so we will always respect the wishes of our employees. Exactly."

Lando Norris, McLaren, Oscar Piastri, McLaren

Cadillac Formula 1 Team CEO Dan Towriss, seated alongside Brown on the Nevada panel, backed the same principle while voicing confidence in the behind-the-scenes planning led by championship officials.

"We have a lot of confidence in the decisions... in the work that's being done behind the scenes between F1 and the FIA to make sure that we have a safe environment," Towriss said. "But at the end of the day, I think we do have to respect the individual choice and look at that, but also as a team... make sure that we have adequate preparations to ensure the safety of each person participating in the sport."

"That's of absolute paramount," Towriss added. "We can't put people in harm's way. And so we need to consider the environment, the safety precautions around that, and make sure that everybody's able to do their job and participate in an absolute safe environment."

Formula 1's closing double-header - the Qatar Grand Prix at Losail (27–29 November) and the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at Yas Marina (4-6 December) - has remained under heavy scrutiny all year. Following the outbreak of conflict involving Iran in late February, F1 called off its scheduled April rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia on 14 March. The Saudi Arabian Grand Prix remained cancelled, while the Bahrain round was relocated to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit in October.

Although Imola had been lined up as a December contingency venue, Formula 1 confirmed on 10 November that both Gulf races would go ahead as scheduled, with FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem stating the governing body is "fully prepared" to close out the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Even with both weekends locked in, paddock leadership has stopped short of mandating travel. Ahead of Las Vegas, Wolff confirmed Mercedes employees opting out would face no disciplinary consequences, Vasseur offered Ferrari personnel the same assurance, and the FIA informed its own staff they could decline the trip with replacements arranged. For McLaren - chasing Red Bull by 17 points for third in the Constructors' Championship - the closing rounds carry serious financial weight, yet Brown left no room for doubt that staff welfare comes first.

#2767. How the Lakers' Quentin Grimes wants to maintain his hot shooting, even off the bench

When Lakers public address announcer Derrin Horton introduced Quentin Grimes in the starting lineup Wednesday, the easy-going Lakers guard was met with an unusually loud ovation. Dropping a career-high 47 points with 10 made three-pointers less than 24 hours before warranted such a reception.

Grimes has used a recent promotion to the starting lineup to fuel a career scoring binge. But his official place in the starting lineup could be short-lived when Austin Reaves returns from a left heel bruise that's kept him sidelined for three games. No matter if Grimes gets his name announced at the beginning of the game or comes off the bench, he wants to maintain his rediscovered rhythm.

"I feel like we all respect each other's games, we know what everybody can do," Grimes said Wednesday after he scored 20 points in the Lakers' loss to the Utah Jazz. "JJ [Redick] gives everybody credit to go out there, no matter who it is, to be themselves, so I feel like whenever we get back whole I'll still be able to keep playing how I've been playing."

The Lakers ruled Reaves out for Friday's NBA Cup game against the Sacramento Kings at 7 p.m. at Crypto.com Arena. The guard, who was injured during the third quarter against Milwaukee on Nov. 11, did on-court work Wednesday morning before the Lakers' game against the Jazz, and Redick said it went "well" but didn't have any further idea about Reaves' timeline for return.

In the three games without Reaves, Grimes has flourished, averaging 29.7 points, 6.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists while shooting 57.4% from the field and 63.3% from three-point range.

It's not just the "statement" night in which he joined Kobe Bryant as the only Lakers players to make 10 or more three-pointers in a single game. In five starts this season, Grimes is averaging 24.8 points and shooting 55.3% from three compared with 5.9 points and 24% three-point shooting off the bench. The Lakers are 4-1 in games Grimes has started.

Lakers guard Quentin Grimes, shooting over Jazz center Jaxson Hayes, scored 20 points on Wednesday. (Eric Thayer / Los Angeles Times)

Grimes credited his recent success to finding a rhythm after a slow start to the season in which he was eight-for-33 shooting from three in the first 11 games before missing two games because of a sprained right pinky. During his career, Grimes has averaged 14.3 points per start compared with 8.5 points coming off the bench with 59.6% and 57.8% true shooting percentage, respectively.

Grimes has made a career out of shape-shifting. The 25th pick in the 2021 draft once was just trying to crack the New York Knicks rotation as a three-and-D player. With Dallas, where he played briefly with Luka Doncic, and Philadelphia, he had the ball in his hands more often, jumping between the starting lineup and the bench.

Now with two dynamic scorers in Doncic and Reaves, the Lakers are searching for new ways to let Grimes shine.

"A big part is like for him if he's gonna play off-ball, he needs to feel like he's touched the ball and he feels like he's in a rhythm," Redick said. "So, again, this is a new team, and we're feeling out a bunch of stuff for each individual guy. Our job as coaches is try to maximize each player and maximize the group, and there's a learning curve to that."

Grimes, whose relationship with Redick started in 2023 when Grimes visited Redick to work out one summer but accidentally wandered into his future coach's neighbor's house in the Hamptons, has cherished the open line of communication with the coaching staff.

"It's a good problem to have: a coach that wants to get you the ball, wants to get you into a rhythm, stay in that rhythm that I've been in," Grimes said. "So I feel like it's a good thing. He's really good at what he does. We're rolling right now. So I have no doubt he'll be able to keep me in this rhythm once we all get healthy."

Read more: Swanson: One frigid night against the Jazz doesn't change the fact the Lakers are legit

Grimes was thought to be a strong contender for an opening day starting role next to Reaves and Doncic. But the Lakers started wings Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams first along with center Walker Kessler, and then inserted 6-foot-8 forward Jake LaRavia in Williams' place when the Lancaster native missed three games because of a left foot injury.

Redick has said previously he liked the balance of those lineups: Reaves and Doncic for offensive punch, two perimeter, defensive-minded wings to back them up and hit open three-pointers and Kessler to anchor the middle.

The Lakers' lineup with Doncic, Reaves, Thybulle, LaRavia and Kessler still ranks second in net rating among five-man groups that have played more than 50 minutes together.

Instead of focusing on the starting unit, Redick wants to keep tinkering with lineups to find more minutes with neither Doncic nor Reaves on the court. Coaches think those moments could help other players get into the rhythm on their own so that during the second half when the staff is deciding which lineup will finish the game, everyone will be in a good flow.

"I think with this group and the way this group [is], it's just an egoless group," Redick said. "We're going to be able to be flexible with the starting lineup and flexible with matchups."

#2766. Senate passes BAAJA permitting reform bill backed by AI, energy sectors

The Senate on Thursday passed a long-sought bill to ease the nation's environmental permitting laws and overhaul electrical transmission regulations, a crucial step toward boosting construction for the energy and technology industries.

Senators voted 62-33 to pass the bill, which split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process.

The vote offers a window into the fissures forming in the Democratic Party as it prepares to assume full control of Congress in January and tries to address the affordability crisis that catapulted it to power.

More Democrats voted against the permitting measure than voted for it. Still, more than a dozen — including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. — voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes to get the bill across the finish line.

"It's going to be legislation that's really going to make the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters on Thursday before the vote. Gallego supported the measure.

The bill's Senate passage is a key step to it becoming law, but it would also need to clear the House before heading to President Donald Trump's desk.

Democratic supporters of the bill touted its cost benefits as a win after they ran campaigns on affordability, and pointed to a massive glut of clean energy the bill could bring onto the grid. Opponents lamented rollbacks to the nation's bedrock environmental protection laws favored by the fossil fuel industry and Republicans, and warned the measure could offer carte blanche authority to the data centers undergirding artificial intelligence.

"No big, bipartisan bill is going to be perfect for everyone, but we have a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Working people can't afford to wait another few years for us to get this done," Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said in a statement to CNBC.

Heinrich brokered the agreement with his counterpart Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, along with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

"Earlier this month, Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," he said.

Getting to a final vote was acrimonious. Senators amended the package in the weeks leading up to the vote to address concerns from Native American tribes, which objected to changes in their participation in permitting.

"I'm not going to sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told reporters Thursday about the push for his amendment, which would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands.

Clean energy and fossil energy groups both cheered the bill's passage in the Senate.

As negotiated, the bill would benefit both renewables and fossil fuels. Artificial intelligence and the broader tech industry also stand to benefit — despite the bill's provision forcing hyperscalers to pay for upgrades to the grid — as power-hungry data centers demand more electricity.

The American Clean Power Association, a group that represents renewables, said it was "a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices."

The American Petroleum Institute, which represents the oil and gas industry, called the bill a "major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure."

Renewables would benefit largely from the bill's electricity transmission component, along with measures aimed at blocking Trump from cancelling already-permitted wind and solar projects. New solar and wind projects are often bottlenecked by a lack of transmission able to deliver power to the grid.

Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040. Natural gas exports would rise 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy. Greenhouse gases would be reduced by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040.

"A lot of Democrats are involved and supportive in this deal because expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy," said Rob Gramlich, the founder and president of Grid Strategies, an energy consulting group. "Republicans are maybe less interested in that benefit, but they do care about economic growth and serving new large loads. And I think members on both sides of the aisle are pretty well aware that we're doing much less grid investment here in the U.S. compared to other countries."

Gramlich added that "you can't get to 60 to 80% of our grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity."

However, the Natural Resources Defense Council was among the opponents.

"The House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers," the organization said in a statement. "Lawmakers should oppose this bill and try again next year to pass legislation worthy of the American people, not for the fossil fuel industry and data center companies."

The bill now heads to the House, where Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. Trump also supports the deal.

But as in the Senate, Democrats are expected to be divided.

"Democrats promised to lower bills, cut pollution, and protect ratepayers," said Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a longtime champion of permitting reform. "Voters are giving us a chance to show we mean it. BAAJA does all three. We should pass it before the end of this Congress."

House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, D-Calif., meanwhile, urged Democrats to say no to the permitting bill.

"Don't believe the lie that this terrible bill, exactly as drafted, is the last, best and only chance to ever do permitting reform," he said. "We can produce a better deal."

#2764. ‘Don’t Use Your Platform To Diminish a City’ — Cam Newton Warns Ravens CB Marlon Humphrey of ‘Extremely Uncomfortable’ Consequences

Cam Newton believes Marlon Humphrey badly misjudged the audience with his latest podcast remark. Insulting Baltimore while wearing a Ravens jersey was always going to carry consequences, and Newton warned that the fallout could follow the cornerback well beyond the football facility.

The former NFL MVP's message was blunt. Having a microphone gives a player room to speak. It also gives the people listening plenty to remember.

On his "4th&1" show, Newton addressed Humphrey's remark that Baltimore was "best at making criminals." Humphrey subsequently apologized, and Ravens head coach Jesse Minter announced Thursday that the cornerback had been sent home and would be inactive against Carolina on Sunday.

Newton focused on the responsibility that comes with representing a city, particularly when the team is already struggling.

"You don't use your platform to diminish a city that you're playing in,"Newton said. "You can say whatever you want to say, but it's going to be extremely uncomfortable for you."

He emphasized how closely a player's everyday life can be connected to the community he represents. "Especially if this is the same city that you live in, your family lives in, the same city that pays you."

Newton also questioned the timing. Baltimore had just lost 23-20 to the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday night, falling to 4-6 with its fifth consecutive defeat. That left Humphrey's comments landing amid considerable frustration about the team's performance.

"This is not the time for you to be making these bold statements, big dog," Newton said.

PREDICT THE NFL SEASON: PFN's Free NFL Playoff Predictor

Thebacklash to Humphrey's Baltimore comments had already made clear how poorly the remark landed. Newton's concern was that the damage would extend beyond one difficult news cycle.

The Los Angeles Clippers have found a real gem in Keaton Wagler, whom they selected with the No. 5 pick in June.

The rookie guard's shot-making has been a welcome addition for a team lacking in offensive firepower. He is not afraid to mix it up with physical defenders, displaying his ability to get to the free-throw line.

However, on Thursday, Wagler did not get a single attempt from the charity stripe against the San Antonio Spurs. According to The Athletic's Law Murray, it ended the 19-year-old newcomer's impressive streak, while also falling short of tying Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's record.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"Snaps a streak of 13 straight games to begin his career with a free-throw attempt. That was the longest by a Clippers rookie since Shai Gilgeous-Alexander (14 games)," wrote Murray on X.

The Clippers lost to the Spurs, 124-112. Wagler had seven points, five rebounds, two assists, and four turnovers in 17 minutes off the bench.

He is having a strong campaign, mirroring Gilgeous-Alexander's rookie year with the Clippers.

SGA was selected by the Charlotte Hornets with the No. 11 pick in 2018 before shipping him to Los Angeles in a draft-day trade for Miles Bridges, who was selected with the No. 12 pick, and draft capital.

Gilgeous-Alexander earned a nod to the All-Rookie Second Team after averaging 10.8 points, 2.8 rebounds, 3.3 assists, and 1.2 steals in 82 games. The Clippers, however, sent him to the Thunder the following season as part of the package deal for Paul George, which many consider the worst trade in league history.

Wagler is averaging 12.1 points, 3.4 rebounds, and 3.0 assists.

The Clippers fell to 4-10, including 0-6 on the road.

#2758. Bears-Lions Thanksgiving audience will be huge — and it could have been even bigger

Last year, both of the early Thanksgiving Day games broke the prior record for NFL regular-season audience size. This year, the all-time record of 57.2 million from the Chiefs-Cowboys game is likely safe.

With one small tweak to the schedule, it perhaps wouldn’t be.

In 2025, Packers-Lions attracted an incredible 47.7 million viewers. This year, the looming battle between the 7-2 Bears and 7-2 Lions should approach (if not match . . . if not beat) that number.

The problem is the second game. The 2-7 Eagles are in soft-tank mode. The 4-6 Cowboys have disintegrated into defensive disarray. While it will still attract a very large audience given the captive audience and the usual Thanksgiving routines, it likely won’t approach 50 million.

While the NFL has granted a permanent hammerlock to the Lions and Cowboys for the traditional Thanksgiving afternoon games, a simple tweak would have set the stage for Bears-Lions to break 50 million — and perhaps to threaten last year’s record.

Here’s the idea. Why not install flexibility to flip the start times of the afternoon games?

It’s no different than the usual Sunday-afternoon flex, like the one that happened this weekend when Steelers-Eagles moved from 4:25 p.m. ET to 1:00 p.m. ET and Jaguars-Giants slid to the higher-profile slot.

On Thanksgiving, the late-afternoon game always does better than the early one. In some years, the Lions game could be viewed as more attractive than the Cowboys game. This year would be one of those years.

It’s something to consider. Getting an annual Thanksgiving Day game doesn’t mean owning the window. And given the NFL’s current willingness, on and after Week 12, to flex from Sunday to Thursday or Sunday to Monday, why not reserve the right to acknowledge that, for the two afternoon games on Thanksgiving, the “best” one should be played in the higher-profile slot?

#2757. Puka Nacua’s Rams-Friendly ‘Suspension’ Will Also Be Good For His Bank Account

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua got a very good break on Thursday. Both he and the Rams have to be jumping with joy after the NFL's suspension of the controversial receiver just so happened to coincide with Nacua being on the IR with a knee injury. His "suspension" will be served over the course of the next three games, three games that he was already going to miss because of his injury status.

As if that wasn't fortunate enough for Nacua, this convenient "suspension" is going to be good for his bank account as well. Adam Schefter of ESPN shared the following on social media: "The timing of Puka Nacua's suspension could potentially save him a substantial amount of money in the long run. Suspended players lose game checks, and Nacua is still on his rookie deal as a former 5th-round pick. Serving it now will cost him a lot less than serving it on his next contract, which is expected to be far more lucrative."

So, it seems like this entire "suspension" was simply designed to benefit Nacua and the Rams in every way imaginable. Nacua will get to play coming down the stretch for the Rams as they look to make the playoffs, something that would have been unthinkable at the start of the season when many thought the Rams were an unstoppable superteam. This just is not a great look for the NFL at all even if there is precedent for dishing out suspensions while players are on IR or injured.

Keep in mind, Nacua was "suspended" for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy. This stems from an alleged incident that occurred earlier this year in which a woman accused Nacua of directing an antisemitic remark towards her before biting her. The NFL also issued a warning to Nacua that further misbehavior could result in banishment from the league, but those words ring somewhat hollow considering the fact that it seems Nacua and the Rams have been accommodated in this process.

Now, Nacua will likely earn a massive contract in the offseason, potentially in the same neighborhood as the one Seattle Seahawks receiver Jaxson Smith-Njigba earned last offseason, and he really won't face any repercussions. One hopes that his conduct does not run afoul of the NFL's personal conduct policy going forward, but the fact that he received what amounts to even less than a slap on the wrist for this violation does not make for much of a deterrence going forward.

#2755. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2754. Stephon Castle reveals the highs and lows of playing as the Spurs' starting point guard

Stephon Castle reveals the highs and lows of playing as the Spurs' starting point guard originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Stephon Castle has been an intriguing player over the past few seasons because he doesn't fit into a traditional position. He can play as a point guard, a shooting guard, or even a small forward. Castle has a strong combination of physical attributes and skill set.

On Thursday against the Los Angeles Clippers, Castle was the primary ball-handler for the San Antonio Spurs. He had a double-double of 21 points and 12 assists, but his eight turnovers also stood out.

Of course, it is hard to discount how effective Castle can be. He is a solid ball-handler who can make the right play often, but he can also score the ball himself. He is a player who thrives with and without the ball, which is a fantastic skill set to have.

Unfortunately, he can be careless with the ball in his hands. This is nothing new because he also struggled with turning the ball over during their run to the NBA Finals, and the Finals themselves.

MORE: Stephon Castle shows his gratitude to the Spurs legends mentoring him

Castle knows that this is a weakness in his game, and he is willing to keep making mistakes because he knows he will learn from them. This game against the Clippers was a rollercoaster, but he eventually controlled the game from his role as a point guard.

"I was pretty comfortable. I had a few bad turnovers, especially early. But I think just continuing to slow down the game for myself and trying to make the right reads," Castle admitted after the game.

Considering Castle is only in his third year, there is still a lot of room to grow. However, his responsibilities will only get heavier with the Spurs maintaining their winning form. Castle will have to accelrate his development because that could be the key to victory.

#2749. Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain

Mercedes driver George Russell topped a second practice session at the Las Vegas Grand Prix run on a wet but slowly drying track.

Russell, competing with Red Bull's Max Verstappen for second in the championship in the final three races of the year, set his time right at the end of the session.

The same applied to Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who went second, 0.071 seconds behind Russell, with a lap even later the Briton's.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, the main pace-setter throughout the session, was third fastest ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

The Frenchman had a faster lap ruined when he was blocked by Haas' Oliver Bearman at the end of the Strip.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was fifth, ahead of of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and the second McLaren of Lando Norris, who was fastest in the wettest early part of the session.

New world champion Kimi Antonelli was eighth fastest, ahead of Alpine's Franco Colapinto and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso.

Verstappen did not run until late in the session but was complaining about a problem with his engine.

Piastri will have a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine-part allowance this season.

The new internal combustion engine the Australian needs as a result of a failure at the Mexico City Grand Prix two races ago is his fifth of the season - only four are permitted.

Piastri and team-mate Norris will also use the latest turbo Mercedes have produced under F1's engine upgrade scheme but that comes penalty-free.

That is not the case for Williams' Carlos Sainz, who will take the new turbo but it is his fifth of the season, so he also has a 10-place penalty which team-mate Alex Albon avoids despite also fitting the new turbo.

At the factory team, only Antonelli will use the new turbo. The team decided it was not worth Russell having it as it would have given him a 15-place grid penalty.

The turbo provides only a small performance upgrade and is more aimed at expanding the engine's useability for the 2027 season.

Bearman also has a grid penalty for engine changes and is set to start from the back of the grid.

#2748. It’s time for Basketball: San Antonio Spurs vs Los Angeles Clippers

Welcome to the Game Thread. Veterans of the Game Thread know how we do things around here, but for all you newbies we have a few rules. Our community guidelines apply and basically say be cool, no personal attacks, don't troll and don't swear too much.

They say that all good things must come to an end, but that doesn't soften the blow when it finally happens, and the Spurs are shut down by one of the league's best defenses along with a scary injury in the last minute of the game to one of the only players who was able to make an offensive impact against the Pistons. The Spurs were maybe a little complacent after winning 12 in a row, and the physicality of Cade Cunningham and their entire roster of scrappy fighters disrupted the Spurs' offense for the entire game, and Harper slipping on the court and losing the ball when the Spurs had a shot to cut the lead to 5 points with a minute left was the coup de grace for the Silver and Black's slim chances of extending the win streak.

Dylan Harper is listed as out tonight with 'hip soreness' which is actually a bit encouraging, since soreness could be an injury where could be returning within a couple of weeks or less, and when he fell, it looked a lot more serious than that. Obviously, we are going to have to wait for a more precise timeline, but I feel like it could have been a lot worse, and the lack of terrible news feels like good news to me.

Tonight the Spurs face the 4-9 Clippers, who are dangerous despite their losing record. They're 2-1 in their last three beating the Thunder in an NBA Cup game by one point, defeating the Hornets, and then inexplicably being blown out 132-107 by the Jazz behind Brice Sensabaugh's 40 point offensive explosion. I feel lucky that the Spurs are done playing the Jazz this season, because they seem to be putting things together under Will Hardy with their talented young roster.

Will we see the Clippers who beat the Thunder, or the team that couldn't hang with the Jazz? I think that isn't what the team needs to worry about, they need to get back to themselves after the losing effort against Detroit, and work on more efficient offensive execution and freeing up Victor in the paint. The bench needs to improve their play, and with Julian Champagnie moving into the starting lineup, they'll be at even more of a disadvantage. #2740. Lions' Aidan Hutchinson says his jumping celebration days are over after torn ACL: 'That's the last time I go airborne'

Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson commented publicly on Thursday for the first time since suffering a season-ending torn ACL in his right knee.

In an Instagram post, the two-time Pro Bowl defensive end pledged to come back from his injury stronger than ever and to never again jump up to celebrate a big play.

"I honestly can't believe it," Hutchinson wrote in his post. "I've jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me. But even something like this won't hold me back."

"Two things I know for sure," he added. "1. I always come back stronger. 2. That's the last time I go airborne."

Hutchinson injured his knee on the Lions' first defensive series during their matchup in Munich with the New England Patriots on Sunday.

Following a sack of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, Hutchinson jumped in celebration and landed awkwardly on his right leg. The star pass rusher immediately fell to the turf and quickly grabbed his right leg, gesturing to the front of his right knee.

Maye reportedly suffered a fractured ankle on the sack, though the Patriots have yet to confirm that injury. Yet Patriots coach Mike Vrabel sounded as if a return was possible for the quarterback this season, likely depending on whether surgery is required.

The Lions went on to a 35-10 win. With their fifth consecutive victory, Detroit improved its record to 7-2 and is tied with the Minnesota Vikings for first place in the NFC North. New England dropped to 5-5 after losing three of its past four games.

Hutchinson finishes his 2026-27 season with six sacks and 24 total tackles in nine games. He was also credited with one pass defended and one forced fumble.

The torn ACL is the second season-ending injury that Hutchinson has sustained in his five NFL seasons. During the 2024 season, he suffered a broken fibula and tibia in his left leg during a Week 6 win over the Dallas Cowboys. Hutchinson recovered to play in all 17 games last season, compiling 14.5 sacks.

#2737. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2736. 10 Takeaways: Scott Wedgewood Gives Avalanche the Performance They Needed (+)

Last season's Presidents' Trophy doesn't happen without Scott Wedgewood. He was exceptional throughout the year, and it started on opening night when an offseason injury to Mackenzie Blackwood forced him into a larger role. For much of the 2025-26 regular season, it felt like everything Wedgewood touched turned to gold. He was that good.

This season hasn't been nearly as fortunate. Wedgewood entered Thursday's matchup against the Anaheim Ducks with a 1-3-2 record through six starts. He won his first game, then went five consecutive starts without a victory, four of them on the road, before getting another opportunity at home against the Ducks.

Credit to Wedgewood for bouncing back in the best possible way. The Avalanche are going to need him more as the season progresses, and this could be the game that gets him out of his early-season slump.

Read NextPostgame Reaction: Avalanche Put an End to Cutter Gauthier's Scoring Streak

1. Wedgewood made 25 saves, earning his first victory since Oct. 8. In his previous six starts, including that win in Calgary, Wedgewood had allowed three, two, three, six, four and four goals, respectively. Thursday marked the first time he allowed fewer than two. For comparison, last season, he allowed one goal in five of his first six starts.

2. Wedgewood spoke postgame about adjusting to a different workload this season.

"It's been tough resetting the mind from obviously playing as much as I did to just once a week," Wedgewood said. "That was my role, and I got to find a way to do it, and obviously did it tonight."

3. I really liked the way the third period began for the Avs. As expected, the Ducks came out with plenty of jump while trailing 3-0. Wedgewood stood his ground and kept them off the scoresheet. But the play quickly transitioned to the other end, and suddenly it was Colorado firing away. Noah Juulsen had a couple of clappers from the point, and all five guys were cycling the puck to keep the attack going.

4. Remember the brutal faceoff woes in Utah on Wednesday night? The Avalanche finished 27-for-52 in the dot against the Ducks. Much better.

5. Credit to Nazem Kadri. I thought he had a spectacular game. He was forechecking well, relentless on the attack and creative with the puck. There were a few plays where I thought for sure he was going to shoot, only for him to find an open teammate in a better position. He had that 'Naz' swagger and confidence in this one.

Read NextWhy I'm Excited to Bring My Angle to Colorado Hockey Now

6. The penalty kill continues to be great. Even when nothing else was going right in Utah, the PK stepped up. Against the Ducks, the Avalanche went 3-for-3 on the penalty kill, including two consecutive uneventful power plays for Anaheim in the second period. The Ducks had another opportunity in the third, but Wedgewood was the best penalty killer on the ice for those two minutes.

7. When Devon Toews was credited with the secondary assist on Brock Nelson's power-play goal, I wondered if this was the fastest he had reached 20 points to start a season in his career. He has 21 points through 23 games after later adding a goal.

So I did some research, and it's not. In the 2021-22 season, which I often forget was ridiculously incredible, Toews reached 20 points in just 15 games. This is now his second-fastest start to 20 points, but it's still eight games off his career mark.

8. Anaheim's best chance in the third? Cutter Gauthier hitting the post behind Wedgewood on the power play. That was the closest he came to extending his 10-game goal-scoring streak. It's great that Wedgewood gets to be the goalie of record who put an end to that run.

"I skated with him this summer, and you know, oddly enough, he went low glove off the post there, and usually he goes high," Wedgewood said of Gauthier. "So I was sitting on it, but yeah, we were joking. He wanted one. He was trying to get in my head. He wanted one, but yeah, to slow him down like we did that's a team shutout as there's ever going to get."

9. Nic Roy chimed in on Wedgewood's performance. As you know, Wedgewood is a very popular teammate in the room.

"Oh, he was big tonight. We know they have a team that can score a lot of goals," Roy said. "Obviously, we see Gauthier in the last few weeks, scores, well every game, I guess. But they got a really good offense, and when we needed Wedge, he had some big saves. So it's good for him. Good for us."

10. Nelson recorded his first two-goal game of the season. Aside from the Utah game, he's been great on the top line since Nathan MacKinnon went down.

#2735. Research moves closer to identifying CTE in living patients

The ability to detect CTE only through autopsies prevents football players from knowing whether they have it during their careers. Work continues to change that.

Via ESPN, a pair of studies published by The Journal of the American Medical Association show that a new blood test could detect advanced stages of CTE in a living patient.

A study from Boston University and Banner Health was based on blood drawn from a small sample of former players during their lifetimes. Autopsies performed after they died showed that they had CTE. The researchers then found a marker for CTE based on the levels of a specific type of protein in their blood.

“I’m cautiously optimistic that we can really understand this finding and move it forward in the next five years or so,” Dr. Michael Alosco, one of the authors of the study, told ESPN. Alosco described the test as a “game changer.”

The study applies only to advanced stages of CTE.

“We are still in the discovery phase and it’s a small sample size,” Alosco said in a statement released regarding the study. “But if future studies validate these findings, this blood test will allow us to detect CTE with a high level of accuracy and open the doors to clinical trials and treatment.”

The ultimate goal remains developing a test that would show any degree of CTE in a living patient. It would allow football players to know whether they already have CTE, and possibly the extent of the disease.

Football players would first have to decide whether they want to know if they have CTE and, if they do, whether they will keep playing.

More broadly, football leagues at every level would have to decide whether players would be prevented from participating if they have CTE.

The development of a test to diagnose CTE could also lead to research aimed at identifying potential treatments for it.

Where the work leads will be determined over time. And the knowledge acquired by football players will allow for informed — if not complicated — decisions as to whether they will choose to keep playing, and whether they will be medically cleared to do so.

#2732. Karl-Anthony Towns letting his Knicks play speak loudest in face of uncertainty

MINNEAPOLIS — In his own words, this should be an uncomfortable situation for Karl-Anthony Towns.

Regardless, it's produced some of the best basketball of his career.

Before the season, when Towns still was publicly pushing for a contract extension from the Knicks, he said he wanted his long-term future settled "so I can feel as comfortable as possible." Without a new deal, he said, "there's no comfortability to be had."

Karl-Anthony Towns rises up for a rebound during the Knicks' win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026, in Toronto. NBAE via Getty Images

That new deal, of course, never materialized, as the Knicks shut down all extension negotiations for the season while navigating owner James Dolan's mandate to stay under the second apron. It left Towns in that uncomfortable situation.

He's responded by making a loud statement to Knicks brass with his play.

"I got a job to do, at the end of the day," Towns said before the team's game against the Timberwolves on Thursday. "I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what's best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I'm just here to do my job."

Towns entered Thursday night's game averaging 21.2 points, 3.9 assists and a league-high 14.1 rebounds while shooting 54.5 percent from the field and 40.0 percent from 3-point range.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a pass while being defended by Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

He has been by far the most consistently strong performer through the Knicks' rocky first few weeks of their championship defense.

He's shown no signs of letting that discomfort affect him. If anything, it is fueling him.

"I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates," Towns said. "So, that's all I really think about."

Towns' standout performances came just as he returned to Minnesota, where he spent the first nine years of his career.

He didn't want to opine Thursday about whether winning a championship with the Knicks validates the move for New York and means it won the blockbuster trade with the Timberwolves, which sent Julius Randle and Donte DiVincenzo back to Minnesota.

But at this point, it's a clear Knicks win.

Karl-Anthony Towns looks to make a move on Collin Murray-Boyles during the Knicks' road win over the Raptors on Nov. 17, 2026. Dan Hamilton-Imagn Images

But it doesn't make being back any less emotional for Towns, who still has a painting of him and his mother and father hugging that the Timberwolves gifted him. They were the last team he played for before his mother passed away during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"I still have so much love for this place," Towns said. "It doesn't go away. I think it's actually grown as I've been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she's in high school. It's a different part of life, but it's a part of life that I really enjoy."

Thursday was the third time Towns returned as an opponent. But it was the first time as a champion.

"It's always great to be home and to be back here," Towns said. "Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it's special to be back. Obviously, it's bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven't seen an NBA championship here. But it's great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here."

#2728. AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."

Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.

The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."

CNBC did not independently verify this information.

Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."

The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.

"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."

Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

#2724. NBA Trade Rumors: Jazz connected to superstar guard?

The Utah Jazz have given internal consideration to Kyri Irving, according to Ian Begley.

This could also be from the Mavericks' side. Maybe there was a phone call, and the Mavericks want to drive up any potential offer for Irving.

And would Irving be happy to join the Jazz in a different role?

It's clear Utah expects to win more than they have, and they're talking about how to do it. We'll see if anything materializes because talk is just talk until someone gets desperate.

#2723. Kirk Cousins on possibly playing 18 games: "Just part of the deal"

Because Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins was traded after the Vikings’ bye but before the Raiders’ bye, Cousins won’t have a bye in 2026.

Which means he’ll potentially play 18 regular-season games.

During a Thursday press conference, Cousins was asked whether he has considered the possibility of playing a game on each and every weekend of the 2026 regular season.

“I thought about it,” Cousins told reporters. “I thought about it, but added to the altitude, added to the new system, added to not knowing people’s names. Just part of the deal. And, again, kind of one minute at a time, one day at a time, one practice at a time, and kind of keep blinders on, and we’ll look up, and it’ll be March.

“But until then, I think I’m just kind of, keeping it, you know, the short game, if you will, short view in front of me, just trying to stay focused there.”

It’s the right attitude. It’s the only attitude. He has gone from a situation in which he was destined to be replaced with rookie Fernando Mendoza to a team with a 7-2 record and a realistic shot not only at making it to the postseason but also of advancing through multiple rounds when it gets there.

And he’s right about the imminent arrival of March. Given the speed with which the season unfolds, it’ll be over before anyone knows it. It’s a finite window of time and, as Cousins said after Sunday’s win over the Packers, “There’s more to the story being written.”

#2722. Bears work to get a stadium deal in Illinois by December 3

The Bears continue to work toward getting a new stadium deal in place. And, once again, the clock is ticking.

Via Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, Bears chairman George McCaskey and Bears president and CEO Kevin Warren met with the league’s stadium committee on Wednesday to provide updates on potential sites in Illinois and Indiana.

Indiana is ready to go. The fact that the Bears have yet to go strongly suggests that they prefer Illinois.

And while prior reports indicated that a deal is expected with the Illinois legislature, the current session ends on December 3. If a deal isn’t reached by then, the can gets kicked again.

Which, in turn, raises the question of whether the Bears will finalize an agreement with Indiana.

Nothing is binding until contracts are signed. Even then, it won’t be real until construction begins.

The ultimate goal is to begin construction. At the league meetings in March, Warren told PFT Live that, with each year that the project is delayed, the expected cost increases by another $150 million.

#2721. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

Well before he said in a post-game news conference Wednesday night that he was embarrassed about the Nets' lack of effort in a blowout loss to the Bulls, his frustration and anger were already evident.

As seen and heard in a since-viral video taken from behind the bench at the end of the third quarter, Randle admonished his teammates for several seconds for showing "no pride" in their latest defeat, which he later called "one of the worst games I've ever been a part of" in his career.

With seven first-round picks over the past two seasons, the Nets still are rebuilding, but Randle and former NBA champion Michael Porter Jr. are among the veterans on hand to help coach Jordi Fernández avoid such alarming performances.

Wednesday's loss — with Julius Erving and other former ABA champion teammates on hand — marked the third consecutive game in which the Nets got walloped in the first half.

Norman Powell (24) of the Chicago Bulls drives to the basket against Julius Randle (30) of the Brooklyn Nets in New York on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Getty Images

Randle had spoken after the loss to the 76ers about the importance of "punching first," but the Bulls connected for a franchise record 15 3-pointers in the first half alone, and they shot 21-for-46 on 3s in their 30-point win.

"They were living in our paint at will, getting into the paint and spraying the basketball. … I felt like we didn't stop them at all from getting in the paint," Randle said. "As a man, you gotta look yourself in the mirror and come into work and figure out what matters.

Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle (30) speaks with head coach Jordi Fernández during a game against the Chicago Bulls, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, in Brooklyn. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

#2705. C.J. Stroud, Texans take care of business vs. cratering Colts: TNF winners, losers

If you tuned in to stream the Houston Texans vs. Indianapolis Colts on "Thursday Night Football" to kick off Week 11 of the 2026 NFL season ... we're sorry for you. Hopefully you had the good sense to log out early.

If not − or if you're looking for a (very quick) recap − the Texans unsurprisingly put the Colts down in a 26-3 romp, though one that should give Houston added relevance moving forward.

But while we wouldn't suggest one of the worst games of the season will have massive ramifications across the league's landscape, there are certainly going to be some ripples. Your winners and losers from "TNF" on Nov. 19:

Four days after what could eventually prove a seismic collapse at Cleveland, the Texans improved to 4-6 and jumped up to ninth place in the conference − two games (and a tiebreaker) behind the Browns for the AFC's final wild-card berth. Still, Houston's schedule does have the potential to continue vaulting this team past some of its collapsing conference brethren.

An efficient night for Houston's QB1, who launched three TD passes and once again looked like the linchpin of this team. Stroud, who turned down an extension in the offseason, could find the market renders him the league's top-paid player in a few months ... if this keeps up.

If you were smart − or obsessed − you steered clear of football in Houston in order to start running roughshod in Vice City (don't catch any strays, Dolphins). We wish we'd been there to join you, getting fresh tags on that boosted Lambo.

Playing for the first time in nearly six weeks after recovering from a groin injury, the veteran tailback had his best outing in a Houston uniform, rushing for a season-high 107 yards on 26 carries. And a balanced offense − meaning a sustained running game for a team that's had one 1,000-yard rusher since the start of the 2020 season − could really make this team dangerous if it finds its way into the postseason field, especially given how a ground attack would reduce the need for Stroud to carry the offense.

The NFL's sack leader was a menace, adding to his league-best total (11½) with one takedown of Colts QB Daniel Jones while getting four licks on him Thursday. Houston's All-Pro pass rusher should very much be in this season's Defensive Player of the Year conversation, regardless of how the Texans finish.

You guys are so lucky you were liberated from Indianapolis prior to the league's trade deadline.

Houston broke out its new, predominantly (Liberty) white Nike "Rivalries" uniforms for prime time. Meh? Make no mistake, the team put a lot of thought into the threads and tying them into Houston's culture. But not sure they're going to make many non-Houstonians clamor for Ka'imi Fairbairn jerseys.

#2703. RJ Luis Jr. will ‘stand down’ and stop playing at LSU, his lawyer says

BATON ROUGE, La. — RJ Luis Jr.'s fight to play basketball at LSU appears to be over.

The attorney for the St. John's transfer told ESPN late Thursday night that Luis will "stand down" rather than risk damage to the university.

"He said, 'Tony, I don't want to do anything that will hurt my teammates, my coach or LSU,'" attorney Tony Clayton told the network. "What he was saying was, in essence, that the juice is not worth the squeeze."

Luis' decision came hours after LSU president Wade Rousse recommended that coach Will Wade have Luis sit out amid pushback from the Southeastern Conference and the NCAA.

Rousse said in a statement on Thursday that he has "instructed" Wade not to play Luis. He made the suggestion less than 24 hours after Luis had 11 and nine rebounds in No. 25 LSU's 79-67 win over Louisiana-Monroe.

Luis, the 2025 Big East Player of the Year while at St. John's, spent a brief period with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics after not being selected in the NBA draft before joining the Tigers.

The NCAA and the SEC have argued in court that Luis is ineligible because he chose to leave college to enter the NBA draft, never withdrew from the draft, and spent time with two professional teams.

A Louisiana state district court judge in Baton Rouge made it possible for Luis to play in college again when he issued a temporary injunction against the NCAA and the conference.

Luis was not made available to reporters after making his debut, and Wade declined to get into specifics on why Luis was on the roster other than to say Luis was eligible, so he played.

Elliot Abrams, a Raleigh, North Carolina, lawyer who is part of the legal team representing Luis, called the threats made by the SEC to expel an institution for playing an athlete who has been declared eligible "reprehensible."null

Abrams added that it "seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him."

Clayton told ESPN that basketball is still in Luis' future but declined to speculate on potential next steps.

#2702. Lakers vs. Kings Preview: Time to start another winning streak

After witnessing their nine-game losing streak come to an end, the Lakers (13-3) have the opportunity to get back in the win column on Friday against the Sacramento Kings (1-13). This is considered an NBA Cup Game for both teams under Group C.

Who: Los Angeles Lakers vs. Sacramento Kings

Nobody is more disappointed in the Lakers' losing streak ending than the team themselves. After Wednesday's loss to the Utah Jazz — where they put up their worst offensive game of the season — head coach JJ Redick and Luka Dončić were pretty bullish on not bringing up the fatigue card despite this being their third game in four nights.

That alone says a lot about this team's character and their determination to be the best they can be, night in and night out. It's what makes the upcoming match against the Kings quite interesting because we're going to see how the Lakers bounce back, especially with the added stakes of an NBA Cup Game.

On Friday, Los Angeles will see a Sacramento team that has lost seven games in a row. That means the Kings could come into this matchup either very hungry for a win, struggling to find their footing or perhaps a little bit of both. Maybe playing on the road will help these Kings because they just finished a disastrous 0-7 homestand.

Ideally, the Lakers shouldn't need Dončić to score 40 points again in this one because it would nice to see a collective team effort win. In their last meeting against the Kings, when the Lakers came away with a 13-point win, we saw arguably their best defensive effort of the season. Hopefully, we see that same level of intensity again because the Lakers could use as convincing a win as possible to keep their NBA Cup hopes alive.

If it's not too much to ask, perhaps an 11-point win or more, so the purple and gold can climb to second place, with the hope that the Warriors lose their remaining NBA Cup games as well. That would set the Lakers up as the wildcard team in Group C.

The Lakers need to make sure that Darius Acuff Jr. — the only bright spot for the Kings so far this season — doesn't go off. Same goes with a microwave scorer like Zach LaVine and even Domantas Sabonis, who combined for 37 points last time. That was the same L.A. team that lost the rebounding battle (46-36), which can't happen again.

It would be nice to see a bounceback performance from Walker Kessler, who struggled mightily against the Jazz last Tuesday. Same goes with Sandro Mamukelashvili, Colin Sexton and Jake LaRavia, who need to provide some scoring to ease off the pressure on Dončić and Quentin Grimes.

If the Lakers regain their offense and play like the team that had just won nine straight games, then they should be able to take care of this one. Let's see if they can start another winning streak by defeating the Kings on Friday.

The Kings have struggled to close out games, which could work in the Lakers' favor. Ideally, L.A. won't need a clutch-time performance but if it comes down to that, they should be able to capitalize.

The Kings also don't guard the 3-point line very well. In their previous game against the Phoenix Suns, the latter shot 44% from deep.

On to the injury report, only Austin Reaves (left heel contusion) is out.

As for the Kings, Ben Simmons (right Achilles tendon repair) and Maxime Raynaud (right patella subluxation) are out. Precious Achiuwa (left lower leg contusion) is doubtful, while De'Andre Hunter (left hip soreness) is questionable.

The 42-yard touchdown pass gave the Texans their first lead.

It was Stroud’s 20th touchdown. His career high is 23.
