#2694. San Antonio vs. Los Angeles, Final Score: Spurs outlast Clippers in 124-112 win

It didn't take long for the Spurs to get back on the winning track. The Silver and Black didn't amaze, but they took care of business at home against a shorthanded Clippers team. The 124-112 score might suggest that it was a comfortable victory, but it was mostly a close game in which the more talented squad simply stepped on the gas late to close it out.

The Spurs, facing an inferior opponent after the loss to the Pistons but missing Dylan Harper, didn't look as dominant as it would have been ideal to start the game. The pace wasn't great, and neither was the decision-making for most of the first half. Defensively, they had good stretches but also moments in which they allowed dribble penetration without much resistance or left shooters open. It wasn't the strong bounceback many were hoping for, but because of their tremendous talent, they managed to lead by 14 points at one point in the second quarter.

Unfortunately, the lead disappeared as the bench had one of its all-too-familiar poor runs. In all fairness, however, the second unit wasn't the only reason why the home team only led by three at the break, as the starters didn't return with the energy required to pull away. Some good moments showed the high ceiling the Silver and Black have, but it wasn't a particularly inspiring first half. The Clippers deserve credit for capitalizing on the at times lackadaisical and downright sloppy play from the Spurs, but a lot of San Antonio's wounds in the opening two frames were self-inflicted.

In the second half, the visitors went from simply being opportunistic to actively hurting the Spurs on the offensive end. The threes were falling, and they were not afraid to hunt mismatches, using Brook Lopez in the post, especially in the third quarter. Ty Lue's guys were confident after coming back to make it close earlier and put themselves ahead on the scoreboard with more consistent play, while San Antonio relied on individual stretches of greatness from different players. Castle had it going as a scorer, Devin Vassell made some defensive plays, and even some of the bench guys got in on the action.

A legitimate blowout was out of the question after three quarters, but the Spurs have been good at elevating their play when they need to throughout this season. It's been enough for them to beat lesser teams, and it happened again against the Clippers. It wasn't the prettiest of games, something that has also been a trend this year, but San Antonio did what it needed to. As the minutes passed, the Silver and Black got a double-digit lead, and they didn't squander it late. Hopefully, it will be the beginning of another long win streak.

As expected, Mitch Johnson started Julian Champagnie in place of Dylan Harper, out with a hip injury. The Fox-Castle-Vassell-Champagnie-Wembanyama unit started most of last season and outscored opponents by over 17 points per 100 possessions, so it should be fine. Still, there were some moments early when the lack of a third ball handler seemed to bother San Antonio. The turnovers piled up as some players, especially Stephon Castle, often forced the issue. The Spurs will miss Harper, which was expected.

Devin Vassell continues to be cold in the outside shooting department (3-for-16 in the last four games), but as usual nowadays, he made an impact elsewhere. Hopefully the shooting touch returns soon.

Carter Bryant was the first guy off the bench for the Harper-less Spurs. In the second half, Jordan McLaughlin got the call. Mitch Johnson is experimenting with his rotations and trying to find guys that can replace Harper's athleticism and ball-handling. We might see different players get minutes depending on what the team needs on any given night.

The second unit has been getting a lot of flak, mostly deserved, for their play early in the season, but they were huge for the Spurs on Thursday. They brought a lot of energy to a game that sometimes lacked it, at least from San Antonio's side.

Brandon Ingram, the big piece going back to the Clippers in the Kawhi Leonard trade, was out with an injury. The other player Los Angeles received in the transaction, Gradey Dick, wasn't all that effective in limited minutes. The Clippers' major summer move had little effect on the result of this one.

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI provided the Spurs' broadcast with the perfect excuse to show one of the best photos ever: the 99 team playing StarCraft together after winning the title. Look at those magnificent nerds.

The Spurs will host the Pelicans on Saturday. New Orleans will be in the second game of a back-to-back after playing the Thunder on Friday.

#2689. Puka Nacua's suspension arises from diversion program

The NFL’s statement announcing the three-game suspension for Rams receiver Puka Nacua didn’t specify the reason for it. Further information provided by the league makes the basis for the ban clear.

It comes from Nacua’s entry into a “diversion program,” related to the incident that triggered a civil lawsuit alleging (among other things) that he bit a woman on New Year’s Eve.

In September, we explained that Nacua had begun the steps required to complete a diversion program, which happened without Nacua entering into a formal agreement to do so. It’s one of the unique facets of California law; namely, California gives some defendants the ability to embark on the steps to comply with a diversion program without the kind of express deal that would have automatically triggered review under the Personal Conduct Policy.

The approach ultimately didn’t avoid the NFL scrutiny.

The suspension of Nacua for three games, with the acknowledgment from the league that failure “to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program” will result in “additional and more substantial discipline,” means that the mere commencement of the process of compliance, even without an express agreement with prosecutors, was enough to get the process rolling.

It also led to a negotiated conclusion that entails Nacua being suspended for games he otherwise would have missed, due to his status on injured reserve. While it all looks convenient at best and fishy at worst, it represents the outcome of a bargain aimed at resolving the situation without full-blown activation of a process that would have entailed a formal hearing before Judge Sue L. Robinson, the person jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association to hear the evidence and to issue a preliminary decision.

#2687. Warriors finish winless road trip with lopsided loss to Grizzlies

It turns out that Steph Curry is pretty important to the Golden State Warriors success. When the Dubs head out on a five-game road trip just over a week ago, they did it with an eight-game winning streak and all the momentum in the world. And then, just a few minutes into the five-city trip, Curry suffered an oblique injury, and a few hours later, the Warriors lost to the Houston Rockets. What followed was brutal: a 38-point loss to the San Antonio Spurs, a 21-point defeat at the hands of the New Orleans Pelicans, a 22-point loss to the upstart Dallas Mavericks, and finally, on Thursday night, a 28-point loss to the surprisingly great Memphis Grizzlies.

The silver lining, if you're into that sort of thing, is that the Warriors looked the best that they have since Curry was injured, despite losing 126-98. The execution was the best it had been in a while, but ultimately, an astounding lack of shooting did the Dubs in.

As had been the case in all of the other Curry-less games, the Warriors got off to a comically slow start. They trailed 5-0, and then 8-2, and Steve Kerr's first timeout came when the Warriors trailed 13-4 just a few minutes in, as the team was racking up the turnovers. Even the good news was bittersweet: Charles Bassey scored the first seven points for Golden State, but also collected three quick fouls.

Still, the Warriors were executing well … mostly. They couldn't resist turning the ball over, with eight giveaways in the first quarter alone, but they were creating things on offense and getting good looks. Unfortunately, the good looks weren't falling, and they weren't able to do much on defense. Even with a nice run to end the opening frame, the Warriors trailed 31-24 after the first.

The Grizzlies came out firing in the second quarter, and quickly led 43-29 with an astonishing 21 points off of turnovers. That, combined with the Warriors' inability to make seemingly any jump shot, made it clear that unless there was a serious reversal of fortunes, the Warriors would not be winning. And there was, unfortunately, no reversal of fortune.

Memphis was turning Golden State's turnovers and missed shots into offens of their own, and used a 14-1 run to turn the game into a blowout at 47-30. But Golden State's response was impressive. The defense really stepped up late, and put the clamps on the Grizzlies with some of their best possessions in the past week (low bar, I know). That led to some much better offensive possessions, with the team getting significantly more aggressive to make up for the unsuccessful shooting. After trailing at one point by 18, the Warriors ran off a 10-0 run, and thanks to a strong defensive stand to end the half, only trailed 55-47 at the break. They had only made three shots from beyond the arc, they had no players in double figures, and Yaxel Lendeborg had yet to make a field goal, yet somehow they were in the game.

It wouldn't last long. For the third quarter in a row, the Grizzlies started the third hot, and quickly pushed the lead comfortably into the double digits. It felt like the Warriors were so close to playing well, but just couldn't quite get over the hump. They would execute well but miss shots, and then they would follow it up with some impressive individual plays supplemented by poor execution. The third quarter was ultimately defined by a distinct lack of easy shots … even when they scored, they simply couldn't get anything easy, and labored over every possession, good or bad. They still couldn't make any threes, and they still had too many turnovers, though credit where it's due: the energy and effort level didn't fade a bit, from opening tip until final buzzer. But energy and effort were no match for talent and execution, and the Grizzlies took a 92-73 lead into the final frame.

From there, it was just window dressing. The Grizzlies again were on fire to start the quarter, and quickly pushed the lead well into the 20s, making it clear that there would be no miraculous comeback for the Dubs. Both teams emptied their benches fairly early, as Memphis rolled to a 126-98 victory, their second win of the season against Golden State.

The Warriors had a serious talent deficit, playing without not just Curry, but also Draymond Green, Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Brandon Williams. Charles Bassey led the way with 16 points, and also grabbed 13 rebounds for a double-double, while Will Richard had another strong game off the bench, scoring 15 points and playing excellent defense. But Yaxel Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski once again struggled to carry the offense with Curry out, with the former scoring 11 points on 3-for-11 shooting, and the latter 15 points on 5-for-12 shooting. While Lendeborg struggled on offense, he played a good defensive game, and finished with eight rebounds, seven assists, one steal, and two blocks.

For Memphis, Jaylen Wells (22 points and seven rebounds on 8-for-10 shooting) and rookie Cameron Boozer (16 points, six rebounds, and five assists on 6-for-6 shooting) starred in a total team effort. But the biggest discrepancy, as it has been for much of the road trip, was the shooting. Golden State shot a miserable 5-for-29 (17.2%) from deep, while the Grizzlies went an excellent 15-for-35 (42.9%). That, along with 22 turnovers, is how you lose by 28 points.

#2686. Colts surrender 26 unanswered points as Daniel Jones benched in blowout road loss to Texans

Houston, the problem here is the Indianapolis Colts offense is broken and has not reached the end zone in 17 consecutive drives. In their final primetime appearance on Thursday Night Football, the Colts surrendered 26 unanswered points in a 26-3 blowout loss to the rival Houston Texans.

Outside of the opening drive, there was nothing left from this depleted offensive unit. Backup quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr. relieved Daniel Jones for the final eight minutes of regulation. Richardson trucked Texans' linebacker Jake Hansen on his first snap for a minimal two yards, then nearly delivered Houston an interception before another anticlimactic three-and-out ended his night.

The Colts were poised to establish an early offensive rhythm after rookie Seth McGowan returned the opening kickoff to the 40. Jones found receiver Ashton Dulin wide open on a sit route against Houston's zone coverage, allowing the speedster to bounce outside and race to the sideline for 25 yards. McGowan followed with a tough run up the middle for eight yards, then Jonathan Taylor was patient enough to let a hole develop and surge forward to move the chains.

Texans' defensive tackle Logan Hall blew up McGowan's next run in the backfield, then Jones was forced to throw the ball away on third down. The Colts settled for an early chip shot as kicker Spencer Shrader connected on a 34-yard field goal to give Indianapolis its lone lead.

The Texans opened with a promising drive, but a forced pass ricocheted into an early break for the Colts. C.J. Stroud's throw bounced off the helmet of rookie safety AJ Haulcy before it tipped off Cam Bynum's hands and back into Haulcy's grasp for his first career interception.

Indianapolis could not have asked for a better start as Jones recognized the underneath coverage, went through his progressions and fired a dart down the sideline to receiver Quez Watkins for a 26-yard completion to march right back into Houston territory. The drive stalled after a dropped pass by Taylor was followed by a pass deflection from Hansen, then All-Pro edge rusher Will Anderson chased down Jones and forced him to get rid of it out of bounds. The Colts intended to settle for a kick near midfield, but Shrader's 56-yarder was shanked wide left.

Despite taking a hit to his right bicep from Colts' defensive back Kapena Gushiken, Stroud stepped up into the pocket and launched a missile down the right sideline to receiver Nico Collins, who elevated over cornerback Justin Walley to haul in a 42-yard touchdown and put Houston ahead 7-3 late in the first frame.

The Colts' next possession unraveled inside of Texans' territory after receiver Anthony Gould took a bubble pass through a hole on the field side for 31 yards. Jones' next pass would have been picked off if Texans cornerback Derek Stingley Jr. weren't out of bounds. On the first play of the second quarter, Jones tossed up a meatball sub into double coverage to avoid the sack and was picked off by cornerback Kamari Lassiter over rookie Deion Burks.

Jones finished 12-for-27 for 144 pass yards and one interception, the sixth straight game he's thrown an interception. Shane Steichen has continued to rely on the eighth-year veteran, despite leading the NFL with 15 turnovers and never finishing a single game with more touchdowns than turnovers this season.

The Texans mounted a pair of long drives in the second quarter as Stroud shared the wealth with five different pass-catchers. Facing third-and-2 from just outside the red zone, Stroud delivered a perfect post to Kayshon Boutte near the goal line. Boutte rose over cornerback Kenneth Harris to secure the contested 24-yard touchdown catch, extending Houston's lead to 14-3 midway through the second quarter.

The Texans were able to capitalize on a choice to send Shrader out for a 62-yard field goal attempt, which was blocked by Hall to seize possession inside Colts territory. Houston leaned on its run game to drain most of the remaining clock before settling for a 27-yard chip shot from Ka'imi Fairbairn to take a 17-3 lead into halftime.

The stampede found some life to start the second half as defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore rushed past the left guard to corral Stroud from behind and secure his team-high fifth sack this season, sending Houston behind the sticks. Houston would avenge the hit on Stroud after a precision punt pinned Indianapolis inside its own 5-yard-line as Anderson rushed inside of right tackle Matt Goncalves to sack Jones in the end zone for a safety.

The Texans took advantage of the short field as Stroud connected with Tank Dell on three consecutive throws for a combined 27 yards to breach the red zone. Houston's offensive line gave Stroud a full seven seconds to scramble outside of the pocket, find tight end Marlin Klein near the pylon for a 13-yard TD that capped off a 12-play drive to seal the first home win for Houston.

The Colts could never get their rushing attack in any rhythm, held to just 38 rushing yards on 17 attempts. The rookies continued to impress on the defensive side as C.J. Allen led the game with 16 tackles, while Haulcy forced the takeaway to terminate Houston's opening drive.

Indianapolis (3-8) enters its bye week for Thanksgiving, with 10 days to prepare to host the New York Giants (5-3-1) at Lucas Oil Stadium on Nov. 29.

#2681. Vikings explored all options before deciding to stay in Minnesota this week

As Sunday’s Mexico City game between the Vikings and 49ers approaches, one of the big issues is the decision of the 49ers to spend the week at altitude in Colorado Springs while the Vikings opted to stay in Minnesota.

On that point, multiple 49ers players have claimed that the Vikings tried to secure the Air Force Academy facility at Colorado Springs, but the 49ers had beaten them to the punch.

The Vikings, we’re told, explored all options — including going to Air Force Acadamey facility and going to Mexico City early. They ultimately decided to implement a plan premised on staying in Minnesota as long as possible.

Obviously, the Vikings could have figured out something that would have allowed them to spend the week somewhere that would have allowed for full acclimation. There are other practice facilities in Colorado. And, again, early arrival in Mexico was always a possibility.

The issue has likely become a focal point of the days preceding the game because of the dramatically different approaches used by the 49ers and Rams before their Week 1 game in Australia. San Francisco went early; the Rams arrived late. And the 49ers stunned the Rams, 27-7.

In that case, it was about time and distance traveled. Here, it’s the same time zone, and the flight is roughly four hours — not much farther for the Vikings than a trip to Seattle, San Francisco, or L.A.

Teams that play in Denver don’t spend the week in Colorado. And while the altitude results in more sideline shots of players with oxygen masks during games, no one ever says, “Well, that team lost to the Broncos because they weren’t acclimated to the altitude.”

The Vikings-49ers game won’t turn on that. If the 49ers win, it will be because they were the better team during those 60 minutes of clock time. And, if the Vikings win, it won’t be because they someone cracked the code on playing at altitude.

But the Timberwolves couldn't find a quality shot in between and never got closer than that three-point deficit. LaMelo Ball badly missed a potential game-tying 3-pointer with under 10 seconds left, and the Timberwolves weren't able to foul the Knicks after they corralled the rebound.

Despite the ugly finish, it meant the Knicks closed their four-game road trip 3-1 before heading back to New York.

Towns had 17 points at halftime, and Jalen Brunson erupted for 14 points in the third quarter. It appeared the Knicks would cruise to an impressive win over a quality opponent.

But Towns went 1-for-5 in the fourth quarter, while Brunson went scoreless in the quarter. As a team, the Knicks went 2-for-14 and scored just 12 points in that fourth quarter.

"I wanted to put on a show for these fans," Towns, returning to Minnesota as an opponent for the third time since the Knicks' blockbuster trade, said. "In the second half I didn't shoot well, I ain't gonna lie to you."

#2677. From recovery to race day in Philly: Former addict credits running with saving his life

A local man, who credits running with saving his life, will participate in the Philadelphia Marathon for the fourth time on Sunday morning.

Between this weekend's full marathon, half marathon, and 8k, a record-breaking 40,000 runners will toe the starting line along the Ben Franklin Parkway.

Kellen Matthews will be one of the 20,000 athletes completing the full marathon.

The 35-year-old told Action News he has always enjoyed playing sports, but he didn't find a love for the sport of running until he found himself at a crossroads.

When he was 14 years old, Matthews was introduced to prescription painkillers.

"By the time I was 25, I was an IV drug user and just feeling all the shame, guilt, hopeless, all the things that come with substance use disorder," he explained.

With the assistance of his girlfriend, Cass, who is now his wife, Matthews went to a treatment facility in Texas. He said that's where a doctor introduced him to the sport of running.

"The first year of my recovery, I ran a mile every day," he said.

Over the past 10 years, those miles have added up for Matthews, who has run almost every race you can imagine.

"I feel like running gives me the exact opposite feeling that being affected by substance abuse disorder gives me... it gives you pride and something to build on," he told Action News' Caroline Goggin.

Matthews has built a career surrounding this sport. He has used his story to become a content creator and to start a run club called the "Recovery Run Club."

"It's kind of for anyone in some sort of recovery - could be eating disorders, substance use, domestic violence. Whatever it is that you're struggling with and looking to recover from, you can come out, find community, and get some exercise," he explained.

Now, he is the face of a statewide public awareness campaign designed to teach Pennsylvanians that recovery is possible.

"I really can't put into words how proud I am of myself because I couldn't have imagined in a million years that I would be in the position that I'm in now," he said.

This weekend, with his wife and daughter there to cheer him on, Matthews will take on the Philadelphia Marathon - fueled by a complicated past that has led him to this moment.

"I often use my experience as fuel when things get tough," he said. "Helps keep things in perspective that I'm choosing to do hard things."

#2675. Jack Ham will return to Penn State radio booth following medical emergency

Pro Football Hall of Fame linebacker Jack Ham announced he will return to the Penn State radio booth on Saturday, two weeks after a medical emergency.

Ham, a color analyst for the Penn State Sports Network since 2000, was transported to the University of Washington Medical Center during pregame of the Nittany Lions’ Nov. 7 game. He missed Penn State’s game against Minnesota last week.

I’ve spent a lot of Saturdays in Beaver Stadium, first on the field and then up in the booth,” Ham, 77, said in his statement. “I’ll be back alongside Steve [Jones] this weekend, and there’s nowhere else I’d rather be.”

Jones treated Ham at the scene, saving his life, according to Penn State coach Matt Campbell. Ham remained in the hospital several days before returning to Pennsylvania on Saturday.

“I’m feeling good, and I owe a great deal to the people who took care of me and stood by me through all of it,” Ham said.

Ham was a six-time All-Pro with the Steelers, with whom he won four Super Bowl championships. He also made eight Pro Bowl appearances. He earned All-America honors at Penn State in 1970.

He entered the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and the College Football Hall of Fame two years later.

#2669. Spurs’ Victor Wembanyama explains hilarious jump-shot dunk during Clippers game

Spurs' Victor Wembanyama explains hilarious jump-shot dunk during Clippers game appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Los Angeles Clippers gave the San Antonio Spurs fits during their Thursday night contest, but in the end, the Spurs locked in and got enough breathing room en route to a 124-112 victory. With less than four minutes remaining in the game and the Spurs already up by double digits, Victor Wembanyama got out in transition after a missed jumpshot Rui Hachimura — setting himself up for one of the most incredibly hilarious plays in NBA history.

Wembanyama, who stands at 7-foot-4, can dunk the ball whenever he's within a few feet of the basket. But with no Clippers defender in sight, the Spurs star tried something new. Instead of slamming the ball (throwing it down while touching the rim), Wembanyama made use of his freakish size to shoot a jumpshot from point-blank range in a way that's similar to how the layman can dunk the ball in puny basketball arcade machines.

But Wembanyama simply wasn't showboating. He did that insane play for a reason. After the game, the Spurs star revealed that he's protecting himself from making the blisters on his fingers worse. Thus, whenever possible, he looks to avoid throwing it down.

"I'm not gonna lie, I've had this blister forever and it's killing me. And every time I dunk it, kills me. If I can avoid it, I'll avoid it. It's actually so painful," Wembanyama said in his postgame presser, via Oh No He Didn't on X.

Wembanyama entered the night with 69 dunks already on the season in just 15 games, giving him an average of nearly five dunks per contest. The force and the regularity with which he throws it down must be leading to those blisters.

Nonetheless, his combination of size, length, timing, and soft hands make him the perfect lob target for the Spurs. They generate so many easy buckets due to Wembanyama's skillset and physical stature, and it will be in the Spurs' best interest to try and help their star man heal from those painful blisters as quickly as possible.

Houston Texans quarterback CJ. Stroud passed for 194 yards and three touchdowns, providing more than enough offense for a defense that shut down the Indianapolis Colts effectively in a 26-3 win on Thursday night.

The Texans won at home for the first time this season after losing their previous five at Reliant Stadium.

Stroud completed 21-of-27 passes with one interception. A second one appeared to be taken away in the second quarter before replay review ruled that Colts safety Cam Bynum didn't catch the ball cleanly.

Nico Collins caught three passes for 58 yards and a touchdown, while Kayshon Boutte followed with two catches for 40 yards and a score. Rookie tight end Marlin Klein caught Stroud's third TD pass.

The Texans' offense also benefited from the return of running back David Montgomery, back after a four-game absence due to a groin injury. The eight-year veteran rushed for 107 yards on 26 carries, keeping several drives moving on the ground. Emari Demercado also ran effectively, gaining 33 yards on five carries.

However, the sharpest thing seen on the field Thursday night may have been the Texans' "Rivalries" alternate uniforms that harkened back to the Oilers' classic look. With the victory, Houston improved to 4-6 and stayed on the fringes of the playoff race in the AFC. The Texans play host to the Baltimore Ravens in Week 12.

On the other side, the Colts could get nothing going with their rushing attack. Jonathan Taylor managed only 21 yards on 11 carries. That put more pressure on Daniel Jones to produce in the passing game, which did not happen.

Jones completed 12-of-27 passes for 144 yards and an interception. He did connect on four passes of 20 yards or more, but that simply wasn't enough to move Indianapolis toward the end zone. He was also tackled for a safety by Will Anderson Jr. in the third quarter after the Colts were pinned at their 5-yard line on a 62-yard punt from Houston's Kai Kroeger.

Anderson now has 11.5 sacks this season, tops in the NFL, after notching a career-high 12 last season.

Indianapolis has lost six of its past seven games, dropping to 3-8 for the season. Yet four teams have worse records in a subpar AFC. Up next for the Colts is a home matchup with the New York Giants (5-3-1).

#2666. Rapid Recap: Trail Blazers 124, Bucks 114

In a game with plenty of highs and lows, the Milwaukee Bucks lost to the Portland Trail Blazers 124-114. On the second night of their back-to-back, the Bucks came out lethargic, but frankly, so did the Blazers. Portland gave Milwaukee plenty of chances to blow the game open, but they refused to take them, and in the end, Portland's vets knew what to do when the game was on the line. On the positive side, Nate Ament dropped a career-high 18 points on 6/11 shooting, while the Blazers were led by old friend Damian Lillard, who scored a season-high 33.

Early on, this looked like a game where the Bucks were on the second night of a back-to-back and the Blazers were deep into a road trip, with intensity lacking on both sides. Tyler Herro looked rough, losing the ball and even missing free throws. Thankfully, Nate Ament was the spark, scoring seven of the first nine points as the Bucks took an early lead. Without Deni Avdija, the Blazers looked considerably less dangerous offensively but still stayed close thanks to their defence as they kept forcing turnovers. Of course, it didn't help that the Bucks, yet again, couldn't make a free throw to save themselves, going 2/7 (!) in the opening quarter. And to top it all off, Gary Trent Jr. went for one of his signature steal attempts on the final play and missed, leaving Scoot Henderson open for three to give his team a 24-21 lead—really disappointing stuff.

It was more of the same bad Bucks basketball to open the second: more turnovers, missed free throws, and bad fouls as the Blazers quickly upped their lead to double digits, 32-22. Thank goodness for Nate Ament, though, who poured in a quick five points—paired with triples from Tyler Herro and Kel'el Ware—to reduce Milwaukee's deficit to just one at the six-minute mark as they went on a 12-4 run, down 40-39. Both teams traded leads for the next few minutes, with Brayden Burries really starting to get in his bag, nailing a catch-and-shoot three and following it up with a smooth deceleration move in the lane for the and-one. The Bucks finally played with some verve as Kasparas Jakucionis began to make his mark, nailing a transition three and a put-back as the home side took a 55-47 lead with 3:30 to play. Of course, Scoot Henderson, who was shooting 20.0% from three coming into the game, went 4/4 in the first half as Portland closed on a 15-3 run to take a 60-58 lead into halftime.

The Bucks started the third with great energy on both ends. They opened with a perfectly run post-entry play where Herro got the ball off a screen for a three; then, a few plays later, Burries stole the ball, and Herro drained another three—this time from the corner—Bucks up 68-63 after two minutes. Portland brought Jrue Holiday in to stem the tide, and, like clockwork, the Blazers responded with a 15-2 extended run. Yep. HOWEVER, the Bucks didn't go quietly as the second unit came in and offered a real spark, cutting the deficit back to three with a few minutes remaining. Crucial late plays from Jakucionis and Rollins put the Blazers up 96-92 after three.

After playing his first minutes of the season last night and making a great impression, Caris LeVert opened the fourth with an elite defensive play, stealing the ball from Dame and converting on the and-one. A few plays later came the sequence of the night: Rollins flipped it to Ware for the baseline poster, then Rollins ripped Dame in the backcourt for the lefty finish, then Burries stonewalled Henderson in the backcourt to force the eight-second violation—Fiserv was rocking! The Blazers would fight back to extend their lead to six, but the Bucks answered with an 8-0 spurt made entirely off of buckets from Ware and Burries to take a 108-106 lead with six minutes to play! But of course, Jrue Holiday—who had made big shots all night—dropped consecutive buckets to give Portland back the edge, leading 112-108. At the three-minute mark, after buckets from Ament and Herro, it was a one-point game, but poor backcourt composure allowed Portland extend their lead to seven, which was enough in the end. Damn.

The Bucks won the possession game by a huge margin (91-77), but they just couldn't convert enough open shots. They were particularly horrid in the first quarter, shooting 8/21.

Trade Kel'el Ware. Trade Myles Turner. Trade Jericho Sims. Pete Nance is the only big you will ever need. Team-high +8 and one of just two Bucks with a positive rating.

#2665. Shane Steichen on Daniel Jones remaining the starter: "We'll evaluate everything"

As the Colts continue to struggle offensively, they continue to cling to quarterback Daniel Jones.

Asked by reporters after the 26-3 loss to the Texans whether Jones will remain the starter, coach Shane Steichen said, “We’ll evaluate everything.”

The No. 2 quarterback is 2023 top-five pick Anthony Richardson. On Thursday night, he got a garbage-time drive in the fourth quarter. The three-and-out, which started at the Indianapolis 39, consisted of Richardson running for two yards and throwing two incomplete passes.

It was Richardson’s second appearance of the season; in Week 8, he got a couple of mop-up drives when the Colts trailed the Jaguars, 42-7.

At some point, Richardson deserves a real chance to play. How much worse can the Colts’ offense be?

The Colts were outgained by the Texans, 354 yards to 167. They converted one of 11 third-down tries. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes, for 144 yards, no touchdowns, and an interception.

There’s a business reason that points to the Colts eventually getting Jones off the field. His contract has a $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027. It vests in March. They’ll inevitably bench Jones to keep him from getting an injury that would keep the Colts from releasing him before the injury guarantee converts to a full guarantee.

That’s what the Giants did to Jones two years ago. He then requested, and received, his release.

The same thing could be happening, sooner rather than later, for Jones in Indianapolis. Which means that he could be available to another team.

That possibility highlights the Colts’ decision to not trade him for whatever they could get. And maybe they tried.

Maybe, in the end, his availability in trade is what helped the Vikings keep the Raiders’ asking price for Kirk Cousins to a third-round pick.

And maybe, in the end, the Vikings will have a chance to add Jones to the depth chart while showing Carson Wentz the door.

#2663. Damian Lillard scores season-high 33 points in first game vs. Bucks post-injury, leads Trail Blazers to win

The Portland Trail Blazers made the trek to Milwaukee last year to play the Bucks. Damian Lillard was present, even though he was sitting out the entire 2025-26 campaign — his first season back with the Trail Blazers — as he recovered from the Achilles tear he suffered while playing for the Bucks in their 2025 first-round playoff series.

Fiserv Forum aired a video tribute to Lillard amid that November 2025 meeting, and the nine-time All-Star received a standing ovation after it played that night.

Thursday marked the 36-year-old guard's first time taking the court against Milwaukee since his injury and his two-season stint with the Bucks. Lillard was subdued talking about the matchup in the lead-up to tip-off, but he came away with his best performance in 624 days.

March 5, 2025, was the last time Lillard had a 30-point game. He scored a season-high 33 points on Thursday in a 124-114 victory over a reeling and rebuilding Milwaukee (1-15).

Portland (10-5) bounced back after dropping consecutive games to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Lillard once again received a warm welcome from Bucks fans. Milwaukee ultimately waived him to sign center Myles Turner in the summer of 2025. The Bucks are still paying Lillard after they decided to stretch the remaining $113 million on his contract.

So, on Thursday, Milwaukee fans watched their team lose its 12th straight game and Lillard shoot 10 of 18 from the field, including 5 of 12 from the beyond the arc.

Plus, another former Bucks player, Jrue Holiday — part of Milwaukee's NBA championship team in 2020-21 — put on a show of his own. He logged 22 points, 7 assists and 4 steals.

Holiday stepped back to hit a crucial jumper with about 5 ½ minutes to go. Another 36-year-old guard, Holiday went on to help the Trail Blazers create separation late, even coupling a steal with a layup.

Portland also got 27 points and seven rebounds from a much younger member of its backcourt: Scoot Henderson.

Meanwhile, the Bucks fell again, a day removed from facing Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time.

Milwaukee had four players score 15-plus points this time out. Tyler Herro led the way with 19, Kasparas Jakučionis and Nate Ament had 18 apiece and Ryan Rollins chipped in 15. Turner, notably, was out with a shoulder injury.

The lead changed hands incessantly on Thursday. Herro drew the Bucks within one at the 3:18 mark in the fourth quarter. The Trail Blazers, though, scored the final nine points, with Lillard netting the last two at the free-throw line.

#2662. After Thursday's loss, will Colts give Anthony Richardson another real shot?

Down 26-3 to the Houston Texans Thursday night, the Colts made a quarterback change, benching Daniel Jones and bringing in Anthony Richardson for mop-up duty in the blowout loss.

The Colts took this approach late in the 42-7 loss to the Jaguars on Nov. 1, giving Richardson a few token snaps. It wasn't an evaluation; it was a cup of coffee. That was his last appearance prior to Thursday.

Richardson, 24, has been in limbo for a few years now, a gifted talent in a state of arrested development, playing for a team that doesn't appear too jazzed to get a longer re-examination of a player they drafted fourth overall just three years ago.

On Thursday, Richardson entered midway through the fourth quarter and missed his first two throws of the night. There was no second series; the Texans ran out the clock. And it almost feels like the Colts are trying to run out the clock on Richardson, Jones, Riley Leonard — all of it.

Head coach Shane Steichen this week said he takes "everything into account" when it comes to the quarterbacks. He added: "Obviously, the biggest thing is taking care of the football moving forward."

Asked about a potential QB change after Thursday's loss, Steichen said, "we'll evaluate everything."

Steichen previously has been reluctant to put all the blame on Jones, and it's fair to point out that the Colts offloaded two notable talents at the trade deadline in offensive guard Quenton Nelson and wide receiver Josh Downs.

But the problems have been chronic, even when those player were on the roster. Jones hasn't had more touchdowns than interceptions in any game this season. He's thrown picks in 10 of his 11 games. The contract extension he signed in the offseason is looking more painful, on the books for $46.8 million next season, although it's a deal the Colts can get out of as a post-June 1 cut.

Still, if we're already forecasting the potential end of Jones in Indianapolis, and likely another pivot at quarterback for the franchise, why is Richardson not even a provisional option at this point? Is he that far gone in their eyes?

The excuse for not making a change this week was the Thursday game and the shortened schedule. But it's not as if Richardson hasn't been here for a minute. It's hard to imagine Steichen sees a whole lot of upside in Richardson, or the hook would have come sooner for Jones. Heck, it wouldn't be stunning if Steichen gave Leonard a chance, even over Richardson, at some point.

The Colts declined Richardson's fifth-year option, so the writing has been on the wall for a bit. It's hard not to look back at that 2024 game when Richardson reportedly "needed a breather" as a turning point in Steichen's trust in the QB, even if he ended up bringing Richardson back a few weeks later. Whenever that turning point happened, the trust level just hasn't been there for some time.

Steichen has hinted that a QB change could come, even prior to Thursday night. So there could be an opportunity for someone. There are six games remaining, with the Week 13 bye upcoming.

But isn't Steichen worried about his job? The general manager is already gone, and the owner is watching the operation closely. Outside of a narrow home win over the Dolphins, it hasn't looked very pretty lately. Steichen is going to do what he feels he needs to do to keep his job.

Is there any upside to bringing Jones back next week against the Giants? The Colts might not believe in Richardson, but they could end up helping each other out. If the QB can string a few games together, it helps his chances elsewhere next season. And if the Colts can win a few games, maybe everyone won't lose their jobs.

The big picture isn't pretty, and the Colts still don't have a first-round pick next year, but it's hard to imagine they can't try to squeeze something out of a player who at least has made some energy-generating plays with his legs, even if Richardson's passing metrics haven't been terribly defensible.

Beggars can't be choosers. Jones is playing like a guy who's less than a year removed from an Achilles injury, and the Colts' roster has been gutted. Sure, Leonard is the QB who might have the best chance to return next season, but Richardson has the better talent.

Can he get one more shot to do something in Indy?

#2661. As NFC South threatens another sub-.500 division winner, does NFL playoff structure need makeover? 'It'll take an egregious deal'

Entering Week 11 of the 2026 NFL season, clubs find themselves asking what's become a familiar question: Will this season's NFL playoff bracket actually feature the NFL's best teams?

The NFC South is trending dangerously close to fronting a sub-.500 division winner for the second consecutive year and third time in five years (the 4-5 Carolina Panthers currently lead the division). Across the conference, three NFC West and all four NFC North teams each stand above .500. If the playoffs started this week (they don't), the 6-4 Seahawks and Rams would each miss out.

The discrepancy leaves some in the league questioning the eight-division playoff structure that has stayed relatively consistent since 2002. For the first 20 years of that reign, only three teams won a division without winning at least half of their games (two more finished 8-8). Since the league expanded its regular-season schedule to 17 games in 2021, the frequency of sub-.500 teams hosting wild-card games has ticked up.

"What makes the disparity worse in the last five years for sure is that we've added another [regular-season] game," one source with knowledge of league playoff proposal debates told Yahoo Sports. "The more you add games, the more separation in the standings you get."

And with the league's determination to add an 18th regular-season game by the next collective bargaining agreement (the NFLPA would have to agree to any schedule expansion), the disparity could only worsen.

What will factor into league decisions on whether to amend the playoff structure in the coming years, or in concert with the addition of a possible 18th game? Yahoo Sports surveyed high-ranking league sources to better understand the debates from recent annual meetings as well as the most likely factors to motivate any changes.

Sources were split on whether they wanted any shift to the structure — and how that shift should materialize if it does unfold.

One high-ranking NFC executive who favors revamping the playoff structure was skeptical anything will change in the next five to 10 years, even if the schedule expands to 18 games.

"I think it'll take an egregious deal," the executive told Yahoo Sports. "It'll take freaking someone winning the NFC South with seven wins and somebody coming in with like 12 wins. It'll take something like that, and it'd probably take an influential owner to be on that 12-win team."

Would the NFL ever consider eliminating divisional favoritism altogether in favor of seeding a conference purely by record?

Those in favor of maintaining the playoff-structure status quo cite the value of divisional excellence.

From a practical standpoint, 14 of a team's 17 regular-season matchups are identical to those of their division foes. Every team plays six in-division games, four teams from another division in their conference and four teams from a division outside of their conference. The remaining three opponents reflect a team's record the prior year. That means ranking teams within a division eliminates most of the strength-of-schedule variance that exists between divisions.

"Strength of schedule is usually the most accurate predictor of teams who are good or bad," a second high-ranking NFC executive told Yahoo Sports. "At the end of the year when you look at who the surprise teams are, and you look at their strength of schedule, I promise you their strength of schedule is weak."

Added a high-ranking AFC executive: "It gives every group of four the same opportunity."

On a more emotional note, rewarding divisional wins with a top-four seed and a home playoff game puts a premium on the value of winning intradivisional games. Rivalries rage more strongly as the stakes rise. The geographic proximity between many division rivals contributes to the heightened tenor.

"It's good for fandom, it's good for the game, it's good for television," the first NFC executive said.

Each of these concerns has reached the NFL annual meetings, from 2008 and 2009 proposals withdrawn after split votes from the competition committee to more recent proposals at the 2023 and 2025 NFL annual meetings.

In 2023, the Chargers proposed seeding wild-card teams higher than division champions when the division champion 1) finishes below .500 and 2) has lost four or more games than a wild-card team.

In 2025, the Lions proposed more broadly to seed wild-card teams higher than division champions when wild-card teams finish with better records.

Excerpt from a presentation at 2025 NFL owners meeting debating the Detroit Lions' playoff proposal.

Neither proposal dared to suggest a division winner shouldn't clinch a playoff spot. But each questioned whether struggling division winners deserved to automatically host a playoff game.

The proposals failed to generate sufficient support to pass.

Sources in favor and opposed to shifting the reward toward record alone admitted: Playoff formulas that dive into the minutiae of counting win discrepancy between division winners and wild-card advancers could complicate and decrease fan interest in predicting playoff brackets. Determining the exact threshold of a change is controversial, too. Multiple sources surveyed for this story mentioned how Tom Brady and the New England Patriots' success was undoubtedly helped by playing in an otherwise-weak AFC East during his tenure. But no team influences the strength of its own division, nor the divisions it's selected to play that year.

"More often than not, it's not a direct correlation that, 'Oh, you got 12 wins, you're better than the 10-win team …'" the first high-ranking NFC executive said. "It gets dicey to try and figure out something that's 'fair' for everybody and passes the smell test, because there are some divisions that the teams are better, and I can acknowledge that."

Clubs admitted during the 2025 meeting discussions that the current playoff formula has limitations, a source present for those discussions told Yahoo Sports. But teams overwhelmingly felt the current playoff structure fit the current schedule format better than the alternative.

A high-ranking AFC executive who believes in the current playoff format questioned the itch for change.

"There's too many people in our league that want to change rules every year and change formats," the executive said. "We have a divisional structure and that is the first benchmark. … I think the history of it is the way it should be."

In the 2024 NFL season, Jared Goff and the Lions won a high stakes NFC North battle against the Vikings that decided the division on the final day of the regular season.

When the league debated Detroit's proposal last year, a presentation weighing the merits touted four main benefits, per a copy obtained by Yahoo Sports:

The end of the regular season would be more competitive.

The end of the regular season could draw more fan interests, better ticket value and better TV ratings.

The chance of a conference's two best teams playing in the conference championship (rather than a wild-card or divisional-round game) would increase.

The main drawback cited: decreasing the incentive to win a division.

The emphasis on late regular-season competition reflected what could be a key force in any eventual postseason shift. As the regular season has grown already to 17 games, with discussions of 18 on the horizon, the chance to secure playoff spots with multiple weeks left to play grows. The league's current requirement that all regular-season finales feature divisional games already guarantees a handful of lopsided divisions in which at least one team has nothing to gain by winning. Sometimes, a game features a division winner with no playoff movement possible and a desire that a divisional opponent wins to hurt the opponent's draft stock. Starters increasingly rest during regular-season finales.

"When you add an 18th game, there's a lot of consequences …" the league source who was present for the playoff proposal discussions said. "[As] teams get further apart in the standings and in terms of draft order and playoff seeding, it leads to a last week of the season that may also require other changes in terms of incentives for playoff qualification or the draft."

These conversations could go hand-in-hand with determining the formula for a potential 18th game. Consider that at that schedule size, divisional games would account for just one-third of a team's schedule. With 12 non-divisional opponents to play, each team could in theory play all three other divisions in its conference if the league sought to level the strength-of-schedule playing field within the NFC and AFC brackets.

"Now, that goes against the NFL's whole notion of trying to create parity," a high-ranking NFC executive said. "The NFL wants bad teams to play a bad team so someone gets a win so that every year they can say four or five new teams make the playoffs. I think that is really valuable."

The league already expanded the playoff bracket from its 30-year run of 12 teams to 14 in 2020.

For now, the league will turn its eye toward the cellar-dwelling NFC South and the not-far-ahead NFC East to see how poorly the worst playoff participants will finish this season.

After that? Expect conversations to continue to simmer, while also expecting momentum for change to remain slow in a league that values tradition and divisional competition.

"I don't think you can change anything until you have a more balanced schedule," the high-ranking NFC executive reiterated. "Winning your division means that the teams that played the closest facsimile of the schedule of yours, you are better than. That deserves a home game.

"Nobody's sitting here talking about the Giants having played [among] the weakest strength of schedule and having a winning record and getting a home game. So to me, until teams all play a balanced and fair schedule, the playoff format is really a waste of time from a discussion standpoint."

#2660. Daniel Cormier Accuses Jon Jones of Using Josh Hokit Feud to Put Himself in the Spotlight

Josh Hokit may have fallen short of becoming the UFC heavyweight champion at UFC 334, but his five-round war against Ciryl Gane earned him plenty of recognition across the MMA community. Even Dana White was impressed by the American's performance despite the disappointing result.

Jon Jones, however, had a very different reaction. Rather than acknowledge Hokit's efforts, the former heavyweight champion took the opportunity to mock him for failing to capture the title. The exchange also carries an interesting backstory, as Hokit trains under Greg Jackson at Jackson Wink MMA, the same gym where Jones spent a significant portion of his career.

Jones famously needed less than three minutes to finish Gane at UFC 285, submitting the Frenchman to claim the vacant heavyweight championship. Following UFC 334, he reminded everyone of that accomplishment by taking a dig at his former gym's latest heavyweight contender. Sharing a post on Instagram, Jones wrote, "Same coaches different results."

ALSO READ: Israel Adesanya Backs Former Teammate Navajo Stirling to Finish Jiri Prochazka at UFC Qatar

The former champion also mocked Hokit over his previous remarks about him, including the viral rap song in which the American took shots at Jones. He suggested that fighters who speak negatively about him often end up losing their next fights. What followed was an increasingly personal exchange, with both men trading insults involving Jones' controversial steroid history and matters outside the Octagon.

Their feud has now drawn criticism from Daniel Cormier, who questioned why Jones continues to involve himself in such disputes despite being retired and having no confirmed plans to compete again.

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Cormier observed Jones' tendency to resurface whenever someone he has a history with suffers a setback. He said, "Jon Jones always has something to say about these moments."

He added, "When you talk about Jon, he has this certain thing that he does where he will have issues with people, he will lay in wait, and when that person has an issue, Jon Jones will then surface and take shots at them."

Cormier then pointed to the latest exchange with Hokit, explaining how their longstanding animosity became apparent following UFC 334. He said, "That happened with Josh Hokit this weekend. Obviously, Josh Hokit and Jon Jones have a bad history, and that was never more evident than this weekend. Obviously, Hokit always goes at Jones, and then Jones has started to respond."

The former two-division champion also felt that Jones chose the wrong moment to target Hokit, considering the performance the heavyweight had just delivered against Gane.

Cormier said, "It was just over, and over, and over again. I could read this for 10 minutes. My point being, Jon tends to come when he thinks that someone that has spoken in opposition to him is down. It's hard for me to sit back and see this when you can't leave Madison Square Garden after watching that fight, regardless of the outcome, without praising Josh for what he did in that fight."

He further criticized Jones for repeatedly targeting people when they are at their lowest rather than acknowledging their achievements. Cormier said, "To me, that's why it's disappointing about the way that Jon Jones actually attacks people, and he's done it time and time again. In most cases, it's when that person's down. But in other cases, it's just a time when they mention him. Josh didn't mention him this time, though."

Cormier ultimately questioned the logic behind Jones continuing to pick fights with active competitors when he has seemingly moved on from his own fighting career.

He said, "Jones took the opportunity to try to come at that dude. If you're retired, you don't pick fights with these guys because you're not going to fight them, and you have no intention to fight them. Hokit goes at him, Jon Jones goes at him, so we're talking about Jon Jones when it isn't really his story anymore."

Jones' involvement in the latest controversy is another example of his tendency to enter conversations surrounding other fighters, even when he is no longer directly involved.

From the GOAT debate surrounding Alex Pereira after the White House event to the controversy surrounding Tom Aspinall's eye injury, the former champion has continued to make his presence felt. Cormier's criticism highlights why some fans believe Jones should let the active heavyweight division take center stage rather than repeatedly inserting himself into its rivalries.

#2659. Clippers vs. Spurs takeaways: Victor Wembanyama adds to highlight reel

Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs remain the standard in the Western Conference and will continue to get everyone's best shot this season.

The Spurs served as a tough test for the Los Angeles Clippers. They gave the Spurs their best shot in a 124-112 loss in San Antonio on Thursday, Nov. 19. Wembanyama led the game with 32 points and 11 rebounds for the Spurs.

It was a bounce-back win for San Antonio, which had a 12-game win streak snapped against the Detroit Pistons earlier in the week.

The Spurs were missing Dylan Harper, who was out with a hip rotator strain, on Thursday. He avoided serious injury but is expected to miss at least a week.

Here's some takeaways from Thursday's game:

Wembanyama can simply do things that others can't.

His latest example came with 3:36 left in the fourth quarter against the Clippers on Thursday. Rui Hachimura's missed shot was rebounded by Stephon Castle, who threw the ball right down the court to a wide-open Wembanyama.

While Wembanyama could've dunked the ball, he seemed to settle for a jump shot inches from the rim.

Wembanyama laughed when asked about the play and stated that dunking has led to a blister on his hand.

"I'm not going to lie, I've had this blister forever and it's killing me," Wembanyama told reporters after the game. "Every time I dunk, it kills me. … It's actually so painful."

While the Clippers still have a lot of work to do if they want to be in a position to compete for a play-in spot later this season, coach Tyronn Lue's team showed some promise and potential against the West's best on Thursday.

L.A. shot the ball well for most of the game and kept the game close behind the effort of veterans Darius Garland and Brook Lopez. Both scored 23 points each.

Garland's had high-scoring performances early this season, but turnovers have been a problem for the guard. He managed to limit his mistakes Thursday, having just one turnover on a big stage against the Spurs.

Max Strus went 5-for-10 from the field, including 5-of-9 from the 3-point line for 18 points.

Clippers center Yanic Konan Niederhauser made his season debut. The second-year player was dealing with a right foot Lisfranc injury and was limited to 11 minutes against the Spurs due to a minutes restriction. He went 1-for-4 shooting and finished the game with two points, three rebounds and a steal. He did find himself in foul trouble with a team-high five personal fouls.

While the Clippers will have to figure out the center rotation following Niederhauser's return, Lue has encouraged Isaiah Jackson to stay ready.

"Nothing (Jackson) has done wrong," Lue said before the game. "You want to try to reward him for what he has done since Yanic has been out. We will see how the flow of the game goes."

Jackson shot 3-for-5 from the field, finishing with six points, four rebounds and three steals in nine minutes of play. He also recorded two blocks against Wembanyama, once at the rim and the second at the 3-point line at the end of the third quarter.

San Antonio managed to get the best of one of Los Angeles' NBA teams, but a meeting with the other still looms.

The Lakers will head to San Antonio next week for an NBA Cup showdown. The Spurs sit at the top of the NBA Cup Group C standings with a 2-0 record. The Lakers are third after splitting their first two games.

A win for the Lakers would not only place them in a tie for the top spot in the group but also provide a glimpse at where things stand in the conference.

The Lakers are tied with the Spurs and LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers for the best record in the league at 13-3. Los Angeles has played well throughout November but had its nine-game winning streak snapped against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

The upcoming Spurs-Lakers matchup will provide a glimpse at two of the league's early MVP front-runners on the court together. Luka Doncic is averaging a league-leading 38.1 points per game along with 7.6 assists and 7.0 rebounds. Wembanyama is averaging 28.4 points, 12.0 rebounds and a league-best 4.1 blocks per game.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Clippers vs. Spurs takeaways: Victor Wembanyama adds to highlight reel

#2658. Rockets' Marcus Smart suspended three games for punching Warriors' Charles Bassey during in-game scuffle

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA has suspended Houston Rockets guard Marcus Smart for three games for "throwing a punch that made contact with the face" of Golden State Warriors big man Charles Bassey, the league announced on Thursday.

The incident came late in the third quarter of Wednesday night's game in Houston. After Smart and Bassey got tangled up on the other end of the floor, Smart chased Bassey down and threw a punch at his head area. They were quickly broken up from there, and Smart was eventually ejected from the game with a flagrant-2 foul. Despite his absence, the Rockets went on to win the game, 115-108.

MARCUS SMART PUNCHES CHARLES BASSEY 😳 pic.twitter.com/MUsLlDHCz4

What triggered the incident? "I just talked to [Smart]. He said they got wrapped up, and [Smart]'s elbow that he hurt got bent up," Rockets coach Ime Udoka said after the game. "So, [Smart] said something to him. Bassey said, 'What are you going to do?' And he did it."

Bassey, on the other hand, blamed Smart for what happened. "He's been playing dirty the whole game," the Warriors big man said. "In the first half, I was trying to set a screen and he grabbed my knee. So I mean, he was playing dirty. [On the play in question], I think I was trying to get a rebound and he was grabbing my hand and I was trying to run back on defense. ... And then he got up on me and swung. Obviously that was weak. I think that was, honestly, fake toughness."

Charles Bassey on Marcus Smart throwing a punch at him: “Fake toughness.”“I don’t think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game.” pic.twitter.com/ZxbgvUDeY9

As for what sort of words were exchanged between Smart and Bassey? "He said something to me," Bassey explained. "He said something like, 'Hey, don't do that.' I said, 'Do what?' It's a grown-man's league."

Smart is no stranger to NBA discipline. He has 12 ejections, nine fines (excluding flopping and technical foul fines) and two suspensions across his 13-year career. Now, the 9-3 Rockets will be without a key guard for the next three games, but fortunately for them, their next three opponents are all below .500: the Utah Jazz, Washington Wizards and Miami Heat.

#2657. Shane Steichen on Daniel Jones remaining the starter: "We'll evaluate everything"

As the Colts continue to struggle offensively, they continue to cling to quarterback Daniel Jones.

Asked by reporters after the 26-3 loss to the Texans whether Jones will remain the starter, coach Shane Steichen said, "We'll evaluate everything."

The No. 2 quarterback is 2023 top-five pick Anthony Richardson. On Thursday night, he got a garbage-time drive in the fourth quarter. The three-and-out, which started at the Indianapolis 39, consisted of Richardson running for two yards and throwing two incomplete passes.

It was Richardson's second appearance of the season; in Week 8, he got a couple of mop-up drives when the Colts trailed the Jaguars, 42-7.

At some point, Richardson deserves a real chance to play. How much worse can the Colts' offense be?

The Colts were outgained by the Texans, 354 yards to 167. They converted one of 11 third-down tries. Jones completed 12 of 27 passes, for 144 yards, no touchdowns, and an interception.

There's a business reason that points to the Colts eventually getting Jones off the field. His contract has a $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027. It vests in March. They'll inevitably bench Jones to keep him from getting an injury that would keep the Colts from releasing him before the injury guarantee converts to a full guarantee.

That's what the Giants did to Jones two years ago. He then requested, and received, his release.

The same thing could be happening, sooner rather than later, for Jones in Indianapolis. Which means that he could be available to another team.

That possibility highlights the Colts' decision to not trade him for whatever they could get. And maybe they tried.

Maybe, in the end, his availability in trade is what helped the Vikings keep the Raiders' asking price for Kirk Cousins to a third-round pick.

And maybe, in the end, the Vikings will have a chance to add Jones to the depth chart while showing Carson Wentz the door.

Steichen's non-commitment comes after a rocky outing from Jones against the Texans. He led the Colts to a field goal on their first drive but struggled after that, completing just 12 of 27 passes (44.4%) for 144 yards and an interception.

Jones struggled to connect with his receivers throughout the contest, routinely overthrowing players and tossing a few passes out of bounds. He didn't look comfortable in the pocket, suffering two sacks, which Steichen noted in assessing the quarterback's play.

"I thought he could do some things better," Steichen told reporters when asked about Jones' performance. "But obviously, there's pass rush coming at him for sure. But we'll go back and evaluate the tape."

Jones' issues weren't limited to Thursday's game. He has struggled badly with turnovers in 2026, throwing a league-leading 13 interceptions, including at least one in each of his last six starts. And the Colts have gone just 3-8 under his leadership, which has led many to wonder when Indianapolis might make a change at quarterback.

The Colts did bench Jones for the final offensive drive of their loss to the Texans. Fourth-year quarterback Anthony Richardson took the field in his place, failing to complete his only two passes while running for two yards on one carry.

Richardson, 24, hasn't started a game since the 2024 NFL season. The No. 4 overall pick from the 2023 NFL Draft has a career record of 8-7 as a starter but entered Thursday's game having completed just 50.9% of his career passes for 2,408 yards, 11 touchdowns and 13 interceptions.

Richardson does have elite mobility, as evidenced by his 638 career rushing yards and 10 touchdowns on 117 carries, and also possesses a cannon arm, so the Colts may want to evaluate his potential as he prepares to be an unrestricted free agent during the offseason.

The Colts also have second-year quarterback Riley Leonard as their third-string quarterback. It isn't clear whether he would be elevated to the backup role if Jones is benched.

Either way, Steichen will have time to make his decision. The Colts don't play again until Sunday, Nov. 29, when they face Jones' former team, the New York Giants.

Indianapolis also has a bye in Week 13, so Steichen could opt to hold off on any choice about Jones' future until that time as well.

#2654. MLB rumors: Yankees eye Alec Bohm, Tarik Skubal books more meetings, plus Nationals, Red Sox, Mariners, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 1 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22. As for the present moment, the General Manager Meetings in Las Vegas are underway, and since there may not be any Winter Meetings this offseason (thanks to the lockout), the GMs' pow-wow could instead be a locus of activity.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace and the ongoing GM Meetings, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Wednesday's supply just below.

The Red Sox are once again shopping outfielder Jarren Duran, reports the Boston Globe. He has been in trade rumors constantly the last two years or so. Boston has also reportedly shown interest in free agent Seiya Suzuki, the best right-handed bat on the market. With Gold Glover Wilyer Abreu entrenched in right, the Red Sox would presumably use Suzuki in left field or DH.

Duran, 30, has two years of team control remaining and he's a possible buy-low candidate. From 2023-25, he authored a .276/.339/.471 batting line with 17 homers and 32 steals per season. He slipped to .207/.266/.361 in 2026, however, and the Red Sox need to add power and get more right-handed. Moving Duran to clear a spot for Suzuki would address both needs.

The New York Yankees are eyeing an upgrade at third base given the prolonged struggles of Ryan McMahon, and free agent Alec Bohm may be a potential target for GM Brian Cashman, according to the New York Post. Bohm, 30, is coming off a subpar walk year for the Philadelphia Phillies, but he has a career OPS+ of 101 overall. He also fared much better in the second half, and his season-long numbers were dragged down by a terrible April. Bohm is not much of a fielder these days, but the Yankees may be willing to live with that if they determine he can provide an offensive upgrade.

As for McMahon, Cashman already conceded to looking for a replacement.

"He's signed through next year for us, but I definitely know we need to improve production in a lot of different spots on the club if we can," he told reporters on Tuesday. "So we'll be open-minded to finding what we can run into if it's there."

The market for ace Tarik Skubal, far and away the top free agent available this offseason, continues to pick up steam, and it may be that he signs his next contract before the owners lock out the players on Dec. 1. The Los Angeles Dodgers, who traded for Skubal leading up to the deadline, the New York Mets, the Chicago Cubs, and the San Diego Padres are known to have varying levels of interest in Skubal. Now, the New York Post reports, the Toronto Blue Jays have entered the fray and emerged as Skubal suitors.

As for the Dodgers, they indeed plan to meet with Skubal, GM Brandon Gomes said. There could be a twist in their pursuit, though; The Athletic reports that the Dodgers are interested in Skubal on a short-term deal, presumably with a higher AAV like they gave to Kyle Tucker. But given the uncertainty of the CBA, would Skubal be willing to sign a contract that has him back on the market in just a few years?

Mets top executive David Stearns, meanwhile, emphasized on Tuesday that he and the club are willing to offer lengthy contracts to pitchers but that circumstances matter. That, in theory, should allay fears that he's not prepared to make a significant offer.

The San Diego Padres not long ago declined their club option on right-handed starter Nick Pivetta. However, they may not mean a parting of ways for club and player. Padres lead decision-maker AJ Preller on Tuesday told reporters, including Marty Caswell, that the team hopes to work out a new agreement with Pivetta so that he can return to San Diego for the 2027 season and perhaps beyond. Pivetta enjoyed a standout season in 2025, but his 2026, while excellent while on the mound, consisted of just eight regular-season starts because of elbow problems.

Dylan Crews, the 24-year-old outfielder for the Washington Nationals, has yet to reach the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2023. However, that ceiling is still there, and Crews is obviously young enough to realize his promise. Speaking of Crews, the Athletic reports that multiple teams have approached the Nats about Crews' availability in trade and that the Nats have not declared him off-limits. That of course doesn't mean a trade will happen, but a change of scenery for Crews may indeed be a winter possibility.

Outfielder Randy Arozarena was the Seattle Mariners' top player last season, and now he's a free agent. The M's, though, may not be interested in bringing back Arozarena and instead may be targeting fellow free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki, the Seattle Times reports. Each veteran outfielder will be going into his age-32 season in 2027, and each produced at a high level in 2026.

After missing the playoffs in back-to-back seasons and trading away catcher Adley Rutschman leading up to the 2026 deadline, the Baltimore Orioles seem like a teardown candidate on paper. However, president of baseball operations Mike Elias batted down talk of a major roster makeover. "A lot of our key, core players are very unlikely to go anywhere," Elias told the media, including the Baltimore Banner, at the GM Meetings.

That presumably means that coveted shortstop Gunnar Henderson, among other notable names, won't be going anywhere this winter.
