#2604. The Timing Game – MH

von Next Generation am 31.03.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 1 Kommentar

The Timing Game describes a playing philosophy in which the right moment of an action is crucial. It not only allows pressing traps to be reversed but also enables teams to break down deep defensive blocks with precision. In the Premier League, Brighton’s then-manager Roberto De Zerbi took this tactical approach to a new level.

“Brighton is a master of passing the ball to the free man but recognising when to pass the ball to the free man and moving at the right time.” – Pep Guardiola

The core idea of the Timing Game is to react to the opponent’s movement at precisely the right moment. Pressing traps can be reversed by first triggering and manipulating the opponent’s press and then bypassing it through changes in speed and direction. Since opposition pressing actions are highly dynamic, this approach is particularly effective against high-pressing teams. Consequently, the Timing Game allows teams to dominate pressing situations in their own buildup play. Additionally, because opponent movements can be triggered independently of the game phase, the Timing Game can also be applied against deep defensive blocks.

Regarding the role of timing in De Zerbi’s buildup play, René Maric (RM) explained in a 2023 interview with SkySports:

„The biggest thing in the build-up is the control of rhythm. If you look at Guardiola, he does it with the speed of the passes and then they carry the ball when they don’t have pressure. De Zerbi does it more with the moment of the pass, the lure, the sole on the ball, opening space with the pass rather than the carry. How you control the rhythm and progress through space will be big in the future. That development has already started.“

This article examines the dimensions and functioning of the Timing Game. Additionally, it analyzes the impact of a team’s own positioning, as well as the manipulation, anticipation, and triggering of the opponent’s press (or movements). The following sections will then explore the action of bypassing the opponent, the potential issues that arise within the Timing Game, and possible solutions to these challenges.

This section is an attempt to highlight the various facets of the Timing Game and football in general. Different playing philosophies prioritize different dimensions. In the Timing Game described here, particular focus is placed on the timing of dynamics in relation to the opponent.

To gain a better understanding of the principles of the Timing Game, the following section presents and explains its different dimensions. This makes it clear how the Timing Game differs from the focus of positional play and relationism but can also be combined with them. Although the game dimensions are less important for the practical implementation of the Timing Game, they can be useful for further developing this concept or other coaching philosophies.

The most important dimension of the Timing Game is the temporal dimension. The crucial factors are the speed and timing of decision-making. The timing of a progressive action should generally coincide with the opponent’s movement. The primary focus is therefore on the exact moment of an action.

A second important dimension is that of dynamics. The dynamic dimension of the Timing Game revolves around explosiveness and changes in rhythm. Changes in dynamics can be decisive both in relation to one’s own play and in terms of directional shifts in relation to the opponent. Ultimately, the goal is to create the strongest possible reciprocal acceleration in the opponent.

In the dimension of individual performance factors, the focus is on footballing competencies such as technical and athletic abilities. In the Timing Game, ball control is a crucial factor, as it significantly affects a player’s pressing resistance. Ball control involves both the ability to recognize a situation and the technical capability to handle the ball under pressure at any time. This skill is particularly important in the Timing Game, as it provides an advantage during the opponent’s pressing phase.

The causal-relational dimension deals with the cause-and-effect principle in interactions between teammates and opponents. There is a causal relationship both between the opponent’s defensive approach and the method of bypassing them, as well as between a teammate’s action and the resulting ball action. The following examples illustrate this:

In relationism, interactions between teammates are particularly emphasized to enable optimal interplay. Due to the complexity of this dimension, I have linked MR’s seminar “The Future of the Game” here.

In the spatial dimension, the focus is on controlling specific zones of the pitch. This is particularly crucial in positional play, where the aim is to control the game through ball possession and spatial occupation. In the Timing Game, however, the goal is to reach the space behind the opponent. Since this space is constantly changing, it cannot strictly be defined as a fixed pitch zone. However, the spatial dimension does play a role in the preparatory positioning of the Timing Game. This article contains a dedicated section on the optimal positioning in preparation for the Timing Game.

In the Timing Game, the moment of an action is primarily decisive. The moment of action is always triggered by the opponent’s movement. The more intense the opponent’s movement, the easier it is to bypass them. This is because, once the Timing Game is triggered, the opponent should be bypassed as diagonally opposed to their movement as possible. This forces the opponent into a maximal change of direction and dynamics.

The pressing near one’s own penalty area is bypassed diagonally opposite to the direction of the press.

A temporal advantage is created over the opponent, who initially has to accelerate in the opposite direction and loses time. The space that opens up behind the advancing opponent can be played most effectively. Representing the functioning of the Timing Game, the principle of “Lure and Shock” could be used. The opponent is first “lured” into the movement and then “shocked” by being bypassed.

The Timing Game is particularly effective during the opponent’s transition from a deeper to a higher pressing setup. At the moment of transition between ordered pressing phases, the opponent’s structure is often lacking, as the distances between the players change. Additionally, movement is present on all positions of the opponent, which can be exploited for the Timing Game. The direction of the opponent’s movement is also crucial, as during the transition from a deeper to a higher pressing phase, vertical movement away from the goal dominates, allowing spaces towards the opponent’s goal to be exploited.

This specific moment of the opponent’s pressing transition into a higher setup cannot be found in the classic phase model of the game according to Van Gaal. Depending on the perspective, it would be classified as part of either the team’s own possession phase or the opponent’s possession phase, even though it is significantly more complex and interesting than other possession situations. The opponent is essentially in a type of defensive transition into attack from the opponent’s ball possession, while the own team takes advantage of this moment and transitions from their own ball possession into a kind of offensive transition.

The Timing Game, however, does not only work during transitions between different pressing setups, but also independently of the game phase, and thus also within the framework of the opponent’s attacking press. The opponent’s movement in attacking pressing usually does not need to be triggered additionally. Instead, it is more about anticipating the moment when the opponent’s attacking press is triggered. At the moment of pressing initiation, there is a very high dynamic on multiple positions of the opponent in (diagonal) vertical directions, which allows the pressing to be bypassed with suitable movements at the moment of initiation. Particularly, the opponent’s pressing traps can be bypassed at the moment of initiation through a corresponding pre-rehearsed anticipation and movement.

Depending on the individual pressing patterns of the opponent, preparations should be made for the timing and manner of bypassing. For example, man-marking in attacking pressing can be bypassed differently than ball-oriented or hybrid marking schemes. Particularly against man-marking, it is important in the Timing Game to initially provoke dynamics in the opponent through various runs, in order to then bypass them in the opposite direction. If dynamics are not created through own runs, there is often little movement from the opponent in the second and third layers that could be exploited.

Because dynamics are also created in the opponent’s man-marking in the second and third layers, multiple layers can be bypassed.

The pressing triggers and pressing traps also differ depending on the type of attacking press, so anticipating the moments of the Timing Game requires prior analysis of the opponent. A very commonly used pressing trigger is a backward pass to the goalkeeper from a higher defensive line. A common reaction is for the goalkeeper to play the ball long under pressure, usually resulting in a loss of possession. In the Timing Game, a team would create passing options behind the opponent through collective movements at the moment the opponent triggers their press. Specific movements and methods for bypassing the press will be discussed in more detail later in the article.

Individual pressing patterns also include the opponent’s pressing structure itself. Here too, individual weaknesses can be diagnosed and exploited in advance. When the opponent presses from a 4-4-2, they often have an under-populated central area. Of course, this cannot be generalized, as, for example, the ball-far midfielder or an aggressive center-back may situationally reinforce the center. However, if this is not the case, an inverse run by the full-back at the moment the press is triggered could be useful to play into the space behind the press against the dynamics. It can be stated that the Timing Game, against different opponents with different individual pressing patterns, influences the movements made to bypass the press.

The Timing Game can also work against deep-lying opponents. However, it is more difficult here because, in general, there is less movement away from the goal, and the opponent attacks in a more passive manner. The deep-lying opponent’s goal is to close the space near the goal. It will be crucial to trigger the opponent’s movement or pressing and lure the opponent out. We will go into more detail on such trigger actions later.

In summary, the following rules for the Timing Game depending on the opponent’s pressing can be established: The deeper the opponent is positioned, the less dynamic movement there is away from their own goal. Therefore, the time window for bypassing the press is shorter. The more passive the opponent acts, the less frequently there is opponent movement. As a result, there will be fewer opportunities to bypass the press. Nevertheless, the Timing Game can be used independently of the game phase through trigger actions.

The team’s formation in possession should be adapted to the challenges of the Timing Game. It should create central connections through a vertical/diagonal alignment. This way, more layers can be incorporated into the dynamics, and more passing options can be created. More passing windows open up at the moment of triggering through a variety of passing angles. In the event of a loss of possession, it also allows for more effective counter-pressing.

Additionally, it can be useful to work with asymmetries and overloads. Overloading the own buildup zone is particularly effective when the opponent closes down and applies high pressure. This lures the opponent and allows them to be bypassed with a few passes. In the linked video example, De Zerbi’s Shakhtar Donetsk uses a strategy of having 7 players in their own penalty area during a goal kick to lure the opponent out.

Nothing to see here, just a completely normal build-up pic.twitter.com/vOcvRPVKdf

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) April 28, 2022

Problems in the Timing Game arise when there is an overload in the own buildup zone if the opponent does not press. The progression in the game is lacking because offensive passing options are not available. Also problematic is the static overload of the last line. If players remain in their specific spaces in the last line, passing options necessary to bypass the opponent’s press are missing.

Another way to structure the team to prepare for the Timing Game is by leaving a specific area vacant. If the opponent attempts to press, this space is usually left unoccupied by the opponent as well. Subsequently, the space can be attacked and played into from the second line in the opposite direction. If the space is still occupied, the numerical advantage in a ball-near area can be exploited. Real Madrid often employs such structures or space-drawing runs in preparation for their actual attacking play with the ball.

In the Timing Game, the moment the opponent begins to press must be anticipated as early as possible. Possible indicators for early recognition of a pressing moment include: the opponent’s approach towards the ball-carrying teammate, the shrinking of distances between the ball-near opponents and their teammates, and the forward dynamics of the opponent. A defensive line with equal numbers or an advancing defender is also an early recognition feature. Lastly, specific pressing triggers should be identified through video analysis in advance.

An exemplary player for effective pressing resistance is Sergio Busquets, who, with his excellent ball control, was regularly able to anticipate and resolve pressing situations. In this 2017 article, TR and MR wrote about Busquets’ qualities.

What is particularly interesting is triggering the opponent’s attacking press. There are a variety of very interesting trigger actions. One variation used by De Zerbi is the use of the sole on the ball to wait. This plays on the impatience of the opponent. The following quote and video clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of this trigger action.

“It’s so fascinating to watch (…) when the ball goes to the center back, they freeze the game. (…) As soon as the pressing action happened, they then had this meticulously designed mechanism of up-back-throughs and third man connections (…).” – Jamie Hamilton, 3rd Circle Podcast

— Jamie Hamilton (@stirling_j) January 13, 2025

Another option is a pass triggered by speed. This pass should be played as slowly as possible and as quickly as necessary. The slow pass provokes the opponent’s pressing. At the same time, by the receiver moving towards the ball, the dynamics can immediately be reversed. This facilitates the transition into the action of bypassing or dribbling past the opponent. The pass direction should ideally be diagonal toward one’s own goal. This maximizes the reversal of dynamics.

Another approach is to play into the pressure, only to then “bounce” back into the direction of the opponent’s pressing path. The opponent is initially led to believe they have access by playing into the pressure. By bouncing the ball into the pressing direction, the opponent is forced to continue their run.

The classic way of forcing a passive opponent into movement is dribbling. The opponent is eventually made to press. However, it is also much harder to generate a dynamic shift and surprise effect, as the dribbling is already in the direction of play. Therefore, it is helpful if dribbling-skilled players attack the opponent in order to maintain the unpredictability of the next action with quick changes of direction. Alternatively, passes that bypass the opponent after dribbling in the opposite direction of the dribble path can create a dynamic shift in the opponent.

Against deep-lying opponents, the inside diagonal is a good method to force defenders on the last line to step out a few meters. When the ball is played diagonally from the outside to the center, the central defender steps out a few steps. This can be exploited in the opposite direction. The effect is enhanced by a player letting the ball pass, as immediately after, the defender’s back can be attacked. This move is known in relationism as Escadinha.

After the pressing trigger, the opponent should be bypassed through dynamic, diagonal directional changes. The direction of the first action should ideally not move away from the pressure but rather target, go over, or through it to attack the opponent’s movement. Instead of directly passing to the free player (e.g., the goalkeeper), a progressive, diagonal ball should be chosen.

To create passing options in the desired direction, specific movements are crucial. There are also various fundamental principles for this. The start of the ball action should be as late as possible but as early as necessary.

The timing of the movement of teammates should coincide with the moment the press begins, so they can be available to receive the ball under pressure, but not too early to avoid being caught by the opponent’s dynamic.

Dynamic movement should also be generated in the second and third layers to have the opportunity to bypass multiple layers. Otherwise, there is a risk of opponents from the second layer, who create covering shadows, not being affected by the opposing dynamic. In a less compact space behind the first pressing line, the dynamics can occur in stages, so the layers are played one after the other.

It is important that after an action, the next layer should be attacked immediately to maintain the dynamic.

The decisive action to overcome the opponent can be individual, group, or team tactical in nature. Below are specific examples of such actions.

A feint in the moment of pressing initiation can lead to bypassing the opponent. In the linked video, Musiala’s movement at the right moment leads to the goal. Although this movement is likely executed intuitively by Musiala at the right time, it can certainly be tactically repeated. The feint falls into the above-described phase of the pressing transition from a deeper to a higher pressing line, which is why Denmark’s player spacing is incorrect and the deep coverage is absent.

Brilliant angle of Jamal Musiala’s goal from last night. 🇩🇪#Germany #Denmark #Euro #Analysis pic.twitter.com/xl2MDgvXwb

Individually tactical, the first touch can be used both as a triggering action and as an overcoming action. By skillfully triggering the opponent’s movement, it may be enough to simply play the ball past the opponent or through their legs. The first touch is made as far as possible but as close as necessary to allow the player to regain possession of the ball immediately in front of the opponent. This is clearly seen at the very beginning of Woltemade’s first goal in the following video.

⚽#woltemade #u21 pic.twitter.com/mpdKiB4inJ

The no-look pass can also be a variant to surprise the opponent against the dynamics and running direction.

Florian Wirtz’s dribbles may initially seem unremarkable. However, upon closer observation, it becomes clear that Wirtz uses slight delays instead of flashy tricks to trigger the opponent’s movement, and then he moves the ball past the defender. This is also a form of timing play at the individual tactical level.

— thomassist (@thomassist25_) January 27, 2025

On the group tactical level, up-back-through (steil-klatsch) combinations are ideal for breaking into depth at the right moment. Here, the previously described positioning in preparation for the timing play is crucial. As many levels as possible should be occupied to open passing angles and options. The lay-off play has the advantage of being able to overcome the opponent with simple passes. It is remarkable how each of these passes is played against the opponent’s pressing direction, preventing the opponent from getting access to the ball.

— ファンキーヤング (@funkyyoung) November 19, 2024

Different variations of the play through the third man are also very effective. In the following video, the effectiveness can be admired at minute 0:13, using the example of the left center-back starting in the wrong direction.

Other possibilities in the group tactical area include one-twos against the dynamics, space-creating runs, counter movements, or dynamic zone rotations.

There are also team tactical variations for overcoming the opponent in the timing game. One such variation is playing the second ball directly into the backline with an appropriate zone overload at the moment the pressing is triggered. The preparatory positioning is the team tactical element here.

A team tactical counter movement could also be considered, where all players in the forward zones drop back, increasing the pressing distance to create more dynamic movement. At the same time, a player from the second line attacks deeply in the opposite direction.

One problem with the timing play is overcoming the covering shadow of the first pressing opponent. As the approaching opponent generates an increasingly larger covering shadow in a well-prepared pressing situation, passing options become limited. This can be solved through an individual tactical overcoming action, such as a dribble, a first touch, or others. Additionally, certain combination plays can help overcome the first pressing player. A back-up-back-through combination could be effective, where the first pass is played over a short distance to a nearby teammate (back), followed by an up-back-through combination to open new passing angles.

The short back pass to the goalkeeper, who has moved up into the defensive line, can bypass the covering shadow of the first pressing player.

Another problem could arise against teams with a very high pressing intensity. Since it is necessary to play into the pressure and trigger the pressing, one is systematically exposed to this high intensity repeatedly. However, this can also be used to one’s advantage. Opponents with high intensity also have high dynamics, which can be played against with greater effectiveness. Additionally, there is usually a high number of opponents in the attacking zones. Therefore, it is advisable to attack the farthest free space as directly as possible.

Hybrid pressing can also cause problems in the timings game. Since individual players act in specific spaces, responding situationally to regain possession of the ball, they do not necessarily carry the dynamics of the pressing players. As a result, they are more difficult to play past. However, certain off-ball runs could provide solutions here. One example would be the outside defender making a diagonal run into space far from the ball.

Lastly, there are issues when pressing the opponent during goal kicks. All playing philosophies face problems here, as the conditions to break out of the situation are not ideal. The ball is not in motion, the opponent can organize, and the playing field is limited by the goal line behind. Additionally, the risk is higher due to the proximity to the goal. The timings game would generate dynamics in the opponent by various runs from teammates, in order to reach the opponent’s back at the right moment.

The concept of dynamically timing a play to exploit the opponent’s movement at the right moment is already seen in practice. However, with a more deliberate approach, it can become more accessible to a wider range of players and even more effective. It holds the potential to bypass pressing traps and break down deep-lying defenses. It is not only applicable throughout the field but can also be effective with different numbers of players.

The dynamic timing play concept developed here is heavily focused on the reference point of the “opponent.” Another possible concept of timing could place more emphasis on the teammate, focusing on relational interactions between players. This concept would be more closely aligned with the relationalism theory. Using the dimensions outlined here, different game concepts can be created and further developed.

The timing play should be used as a complementary element to complete one’s overall playing philosophy. It provides a different perspective on tactical analysis than what would be possible with static graphics, such as those on a tactic board. Therefore, it should expand an analyst’s perspective on this complex game by adding an additional dimension.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

I know Pep Guardiola made De Zerbi the leading authority when it comes to the timing game but I also believe that Marcelino Garcia at Villarreal adds more layers to this topic. His understanding of dynamics is unique and is worth looking into.

#2602. Could Tarik Skubal take a short-term, high-AAV contract? Breaking down pros and cons

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The expectation is left-hander and two-time AL Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent available this offseason, will sign a record contract before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Barring a surprise agreement, the owners are almost certain to lock out the players at that time. Skubal is expected to sign before then.

Skubal, 30 later this month, is a Scott Boras client and Boras tends to shatter records, not beat them narrowly. There's a real chance Skubal signs a contract worth more than $400 million in the next two weeks or so. Excluding Shohei Ohtani, who is technically a pitcher but is really a two-way player, here are the largest pitching contracts in history:

Something like, say, eight years at $50 million a year would give Skubal a $400 million contract that obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee and average annual value. Several big-market clubs are said to be pursuing Skubal (Blue Jays, Dodgers, Mets, etc.), who is a special free agent as an in-his-prime ace. Conditions are ripe for a record deal.

There is also a chance Skubal goes the Valdez route, or the Bo Bichette/Kyle Tucker route, and signs a short-term contract with a high annual salary. It might only be a small chance, but there is a chance. The Athletic reports the Dodgers prefer such an arrangement with Skubal. ESPN says Skubal has no interest in such a deal, though minds can always be changed.

With that in mind, here are the pros and cons of a high-dollar, short-term contract for Skubal. Keep in mind that such a contract is usually a three- or four-year deal with opt outs, not a straight one- or two-year contract, and Skubal wouldn't necessarily have to use the opt outs to re-enter free agency. He could leverage them into a new contract to stay with his team.

1. Maximize earnings. Plain and simple, a short-term contract would give Skubal a chance to max out his earnings by making free agency available to him again as soon as next offseason. Go out, have a typical Skubal season in 2027, and perhaps market forces push the demand even higher than it is right now. Remember that, along with a salary cap, there could be a salary floor in the future. Small-market contenders like, say, the Guardians or Rays could throw many millions at Skubal to reach the floor in the future.

2. Chance to set more records. This ties back to the last point. Skubal already set a new salary record for an arbitration-eligible player ($32 million in 2026) and he's positioned to set a new standard for pitcher contracts this offseason. Go back into free agency in a year or two, and Skubal (and Boras) could have a chance to break his own pitcher contract record. The record itself won't be a driving factor in that decision (the money will ultimately decide things), but it would be a nice feather in his cap.

3. Freedom to change teams. Sometimes things don't work out. I don't think Juan Soto expected to miss the postseason in the first two years of his record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets. It's entirely possible Skubal could find his next situation not to his liking for whatever reason. Maybe the team doesn't contend, maybe he clashes with the coaching staff, maybe he doesn't like the local breakfast taco options. There could be a million different reasons it doesn't work. A short-term, high-dollar deal would give Skubal an escape hatch and allow him to head elsewhere if things go sideways.

1. Injury and performance risk. All things considered, Skubal is a pretty safe bet on a long-term contract, though he is a pitcher, and pitchers get hurt. It's what they do. Skubal has had three elbow surgeries, including Tommy John surgery in 2017 and a minor procedure this May. If he gets hurt again, or his performance slips for whatever reason, then he could wind up costing himself in the big picture because he won't be able to opt out and sign a larger deal. A short-term, high-dollar contract will pay him handsomely. He won't struggle to put bread on the table. But injury/performance risk means Skubal could ultimately leave money on the table.

2. Potential salary cap. It is possible the next CBA will include a salary cap, which could limit Skubal's market and earning potential should he go back out into free agency in a year or two (or three). It's not just the cap itself either. MLB has proposed contract limits as part of the salary cap: five years at 15% of the cap for players who change teams, or six years at 16% of the cap for players who remain with their current team. Even if MLB doesn't get a salary cap and instead the competitive balance tax system remains in place with stiffer penalties, that could cost Skubal in the future. This offseason might be his last chance to sign in a truly free market.

#2600. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Celtics win Jaylen Brown trade (for now), Trae Young looks done

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every now and then, the NBA gives us a week that is essentially built around a single game. A total of 51 games were played in the last week, but come on, the one you remember was Jaylen Brown's long-awaited reunion with Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers squared off in a battle of the Eastern Conference's two top seeds on Tuesday, and even if the game fell short of our basketball expectations, it provided more than enough beef to sate us. Brown snubbed Tatum before the game. Paul George gave a fan the middle finger. Appropriate animosity has returned to this eternal rivalry.

So... how did we handle that from a winners and losers perspective? Well, Boston is an obvious winner, but Brown escaped loser status. It's winners and losers of the week. Philly won its two other games this week, and Brown led all scorers in Sunday's win with 31 points. He certainly lost on Tuesday. He may yet wind up losing the trade. But we're not docking him a whole week for a single poor performance. So if Brown escaped the loser's section, who made it? And who joins Boston in the winner's circle? Let's look back at the week that was.

Boston's big win over Philadelphia underlined something that's been evident all season: Paul George, at least thus far, has been better as a Celtic than Jaylen Brown has been as a 76er. There are obviously circumstantial reasons for that. George is at his best as a force-multiplier, and he's on a team on which he doesn't need to play an enormous role. Brown is at his best as a floor-raiser, but he's on a team full of floor-raisers. That doesn't mean Philadelphia regrets the trade -- it got them LeBron James! -- but it does suggest that, after months of criticism, the Celtics at least got what they were looking for out of the deal.

Everything the Celtics were good at a year ago, they're still good at. They were one of the NBA's best shooting teams last season, and George both makes more 3s than Brown and takes far more of them. They were great at protecting the basket last season and George's activity as a helper has been a net benefit to their rim-protection.

Yet George's presence has also been the catalyst for improvement in a few other key areas. Boston never generated turnovers defensively last season and they do this year, in part because George is averaging the sixth-most steals and third-most deflections in the NBA. They're getting to the line at a roughly league-average rate, in part because the ball doesn't stick to George as it so often did Brown. It's easier to get defenses in rotation with the ball moving and 3-pointers flying. Tatum has benefited enormously in this respect with a career-best 46% free-throw rate.

Again, the 76ers are perfectly happy with their end of the deal. They traded old for young. They got James on the minimum. They're 11-3. But Boston emerged with the player who has made a bigger difference thus far this season, and it got two first-round draft assets in the process. That doesn't mean the Celtics necessarily win the trade in the long run, but it does suggest, unsurprisingly, that Brad Stevens understood his own team and what it needed better than the rest of us.

Well, they haven't lost in three weeks... so this feels overdue. Let's talk about the much ballyhooed three-guard lineup for a moment. The Spurs couldn't keep bringing Dylan Harper off the bench this season. He's simply too good and too important to their future to risk alienating. They couldn't bench De'Aaron Fox immediately either. Former All-Stars tend to take such decisions as a sign of disrespect, and such a move could have splintered the locker room.

So the Spurs made the somewhat awkward decision to start the three of them together. The season's second game, a loss to the Houston Rockets, showcased exactly why so many feared the fit of the three of them together. Three iffy guard-sized shooters minimized spacing for the sake of redundant ball-handling, and the Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle trio got outscored by 12 points in a four-point defeat. Well, the three guards haven't lost their minutes together in a single game since then. They're +112 in 115 minutes after that point.

Now, there are notable caveats here. Every three-man combination of Spurs that has played at least 100 minutes since then is firmly positive, and the three guards have literally not played a single minute together this season that did not come alongside Victor Wembanyama. It's entirely possible that Wembanyama is so game-breaking that any lineup he's a part of is an almost automatic winner. But that would work in favor of the three guards here. Maybe San Antonio is so much more talented than the field that it can afford to play suboptimal lineups for the sake of maintaining harmony in the locker room.

That may prove more challenging late in a playoff series, but it's easier to convince players to change their roles for, say, Game 5 of the Western Conference Finals than it is in November or December. The Spurs might have to think harder about this in a field that included a healthy Oklahoma City, but with the Thunder compromised, San Antonio is such a large favorite to win the Western Conference that it can afford to try to just out-talent everyone else. So far, it's clearly working.

We are in all-out panic mode over the state of Cleveland's starting lineup. James Harden can't get to the rim anymore. Donovan Mitchell just signed a supermax extension that already feels iffy. Peyton Watson's shooting has fallen off a cliff and he's struggling as a primary point-of-attack defender. The Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen partnership is getting crushed in its joint minutes. The starters have played 99 minutes together and lost those minutes by 24 points. No five-man unit that has played that many minutes has been outscored by more. Malaise doesn't do this core justice. Clearly, something here has to change.

Fortunately, there appear to be some internal solutions here. After FAA issues forced the Cavaliers to spend Friday night in Miami, Mitchell called for Saturday's game against the Dallas Mavericks to be postponed. The Cavaliers didn't arrive in Dallas until around noon on Saturday. The starters sat out. Cleveland won the game by 10 against a healthy, playoff-caliber opponent. Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson all scored between 18 and 24 points.

This wasn't a one-off. Thomas is outscoring Harden and Mobley on a per-minute basis. Proctor is sporting a better-than-6-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio on the season, and Synergy Sports rates him in the 100th percentile on spot-up efficiency and the 96th in pick-and-rolls, including passes, in terms of points per possession. Tyson breathes life into a transition offense that is otherwise a sore spot. Most of this team's energy comes from the bench.

What exactly the solution here is, we can't say. It will involve a trade. Perhaps a few. But there's something here, and the early indications are that things are going to get better for the team as a whole when it eventually starts leaning on these players a bit more.

Dejounte Murray requested a trade this week. That's not a rumor. The Pelicans publicly acknowledged it and Murray retweeted the news from ESPN. Meanwhile, after Monday's loss to the Golden State Warriors, Jordan Poole was asked if he would ever come back to the team with which he started his career. He answered "yes." Players tend to not be that definitive in those statements, nor do they tend to acknowledge that their former team "just feels like home." It certainly seems as though there's somewhere he'd rather be than New Orleans.

To borrow a phrase from social media user Nathan Calvin, "if you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." Essentially... if two players seem this eager to flee, more probably do as well. Sam Amick suggested in a radio interview over the summer that Trey Murphy would like to play elsewhere. There has been plenty of speculation about other Pelicans as well. A 4-10 start following 26- and 21-win seasons tends to do that.

We're more than a year into Joe Dumars' reign as head of basketball operations and there's no discernible plan here. Virtually every key player from last year's roster was retained and the team has largely been healthier than it was a year ago, but they're on pace for a worse record under new head coach Jamahl Mosley. The sad thing is that the Pelicans have a fair number of valuable players. They've just assembled those players so carelessly that they've become far less than the sum of their parts. This team is incoherent, and even the players seem to know it.

Trae Young was held scoreless in 26 minutes on Sunday. It was the first time he's been held scoreless in his entire NBA career, but it may be the final straw of a trend that has been bubbling for some time: Trae Young is simply no longer a star-level scorer. He currently has his lowest shooting percentage from both 2-point and 3-point range in a single season. He lacks the burst to get to the rim or beat mismatches consistently anymore, and he's never developed comfort as a catch-and-shooter. Aside from free throws, it's basically all jumpers off the dribble and floaters, neither of which he's making at the rate he needs to in order to justify his defensive shortcomings. He scored 37 points against Detroit last Monday, but needed 17 free throws to get there on less than 35% shooting from the floor. He needs whistles right now.

This is a version of Young who probably shouldn't monopolize an offense, yet he's never shown that he's capable of playing differently. The Wizards are spending 26 possessions a game on shots Young generates either for himself or a teammate out of pick-and-roll, more than any other player in the league, per Synergy Sports. As of Sunday, he and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were tied for the league lead among starters in average seconds possessing the ball per touch, per NBA.com tracking data. The younger players who represent the future of this organization are spending a whole lot of time watching someone else dribble. Nobody is really spacing the floor for anyone else since there's so little shooting on this roster. The Wizards have played close to neutral when Young rests, but are getting outscored by more than 10 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor. That difference is almost entirely offensive, yet Young remains the same defensive liability he's always been.

This is where the four-year max contract Washington bewilderingly gave Young becomes so destructive. The basic notion of acquiring a high-end point guard to serve as an offensive organizer for these young wings made sense on paper, but they committed to him essentially sight unseen. He played five mostly meaningless games in a tanking season and they paid him max money without really knowing how he'd fit with the team they were building. If he'd walked for nothing in free agency, well, it's not as though they spent picks to get him. Now they're stuck paying star-level money for a non-star-level player who probably can't meaningfully scale down his involvement in the offense because he just doesn't provide much value when any other player on either team has the basketball.

There are a lot of things going wrong in Washington right now, but Young is inevitably going to be the face of those struggles because he's the player the Wizards just bewilderingly gave a four-year max contract to in order to re-sign. Jaylen Brown had the loudest individual loss of the week, but he at least won all of his other games and has largely been what his team has asked him to be. Young went winless this week, had a scoreless game, and maintained his mostly disappointing season-long performance.

If you would have heard "the Warriors have a -2.4 net rating a month into the 2026-27 season," you probably would have shrugged and said, "sure, sounds about right." The Warriors were widely pegged as a low-end Play-In, high-end lottery team before the season, and a -2.4 net rating projects out to a win total in the 30s. Except that isn't Golden State's net rating. It's Golden State's net rating in the minutes Stephen Curry has missed this season.

That's how far above expectations Golden State was playing during its eight-game winning streak. The Curry-off version of the team was around average; the Curry-on version of the team was a juggernaut. The latter feels a bit unsustainable, but we won't know again for around a month. The former is what's about to be tested now that Curry has an oblique abdominal tear. The Spurs hardly represent a fair test for a team in this situation, but San Antonio predictably waxed Golden State by 38 in the first game of Curry's absence.

Nobody's asking for another eight-game winning streak. Those wins are banked, and Golden State's season begins in earnest when Jimmy Butler returns in January or February. For now, the Warriors just need to stay afloat. Find wins where the schedule offers them, and fortunately, the Pelicans, Kings, Clippers and Jazz are on the docket in the next three weeks or so. But losing Curry is a reminder of how fragile that streak really was. Maybe, now that Yaxel Lendeborg is emerging as a possible star, the Warriors are capable of genuine postseason success this season. But the health of any 38-year-old not named LeBron James is going to be precarious. Things could be a lot worse, but Curry's injury drags one of the feel-good stories of the early season back down to Earth.

#2599. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2598. Blue Jays' Anthony Santander issues statement after sharing anti-Muslim videos: 'This content caused hurt'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander has issued a statement regarding his recent anti-Muslim social media posts that he has since deleted. Santander's statement, which he posted to Instagram and follows a public condemnation of the posts by Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins, reads as follows:

"After taking time to reflect on my recent social media posts and speaking with people I trust and respect, I recognize that I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared on my platform.

"I realize that this content caused hurt and I sincerely apologize. I should have been more thoughtful about what I shared, recognizing the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

"As a man of faith, it is my belief that every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their religion, background, or beliefs. After hearing feedback from those I hurt, I realize that the content I shared fell short of my own convictions.

"I would like to affirm my respect for the Muslim community and for the dignity and freedom of people of every faith and background.

"From this experience, I have learned to ensure that none of my communications promote hate or give the impression that I support hatred, discrimination, or violence against anyone."

The club had earlier released a statement on the incident that read:

"Baseball is for everyone, and the Blue Jays have created an inclusive experience where all fans feel welcome at our ballpark. Individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

Santander, a Venezuela native, shared social media videos following the recent U.S. midterm elections, including one in which a Christian pastor said, "There is no such thing as kind Muslims." Another suggested that Sharia law would be imposed in the U.S. following the election of Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate representing the state of Michigan.

Atkins told reporters Tuesday that Santander's behavior "did not align" with organizational values and there were no words "to express my level of disappointment."

"I talked to Anthony about his lack of awareness, realizing that he has a very large microphone, what that meant," Atkins said. "We're working exceptionally hard internally to ensure, and we have been, that it's a safe environment, that baseball is for everyone. It's very important to us. It's a part of our organizational values and his behavior did not align with that."

Santander, 32, joined the Blue Jays prior to the 2025 season on a five-year, $92.5 million free-agent contract. He struggled badly across 54 games in 2025 and missed the entire 2026 season with injury.

#2597. NFL Week 11 picks: Our experts face off on Colts at Texans, Vikings vs. 49ers and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last week in the NFL was full of drama. The Cleveland Browns came back from down 17-0 to defeat the Houston Texans, while Kirk Cousins was victorious in his first game back with the Minnesota Vikings. The San Francisco 49ers and Dallas Cowboys put up 86 total points in Arlington, and the Cincinnati Bengals blew out Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers on "Sunday Night Football."

This week there's more. Fernando Mendoza will make the first road start of his career against an aggressive Denver Broncos defense, the Detroit Lions will begin life without Aidan Hutchinson at home against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Vikings will play the 49ers in Mexico City in what could go down as one of the best primetime matchups of the entire season.

There are many, many massive spreads in the NFL this week! Which teams should you pick in Week 11, and which should you fade? CBS Sports writers Jordan Dajani and Jared Dubin are here to break down the biggest games of the weekend. For clarity, lines for these selections were taken on Nov. 18 over at DraftKings Sportsbook.

Dajani (Texans -12.5): I would typically lean toward a huge underdog like this in a divisional game, but two factors have me leaning the other way. One, Daniel Jones threw for just 108 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions last week against the Miami Dolphins. They were starting a quarterback that had never played in the NFL, yet only lost by two points. Jones has been terrible. He's turned the ball over an NFL-high 15 times and has the worst record in primetime by any quarterback since 1970 at 1-16. Additionally, the Texans allowed the Browns to come back from down 17-0 and win their meeting last week, which I imagine has this Texans team seeing red. C.J. Stroud and Co. are better than their 3-6 record indicates. They even beat the Jacksonville Jaguars earlier this season. I think the large number is justified. …  Prediction: Texans 27, Colts 14

Dubin (Colts +12.5): I just don't think the Texans should be favored by 12.5 points over anybody.  … Prediction: Texans 23, Colts 13

Dajani (Buccaneers +7): Jahmyr Gibbs leads the NFL in rushing yards this season with 1,000, while the Buccaneers allow the fewest rushing yards per game (79.2). The Bucs also lead the NFL in rushing offense and in takeaways with 21. With the Buccaneers coming off their bye week and the Lions coming off an international trip that cost them Aidan Hutchinson for the season, I'm leaning toward Tampa Bay with the points. The Bucs are 4-1 against the spread in their last five games, but keep an eye on the quarterback situation over the next 24 hours. …  Prediction: Lions 24, Buccaneers 21

Dubin (Lions -7): The Bucs likely playing this game without Baker Mayfield pushed me in this direction. Jalon Daniels is fine, but I don't expect the passing game to be able to do much here. The Bucs base the entire offense around the run anyway, but the Lions are actually pretty tough to run on. That could change without Aidan Hutchinson, obviously, but I don't think it will change enough for Tampa's offense to keep pace with what the Lions are likely to do.  … Prediction: Lions 24, Buccaneers 16

Dajani (Broncos -10): I don't think Fernando Mendoza wins his second career start in an environment like Mile High, but can he cover the double-digit spread? Denver has won just one game by double digits this season, back in Week 7 against the Arizona Cardinals. The Las Vegas Raiders, on the other hand, have covered in four straight divisional games for the first time since 2022. The Broncos are coming off their bye week and have scored at least 26 points in each of their last three games. Bo Nix has also thrown multiple touchdowns in back-to-back games. The Raiders are tied for the worst scoring defense in the NFL this year with 28.9 points allowed per game, so I think the Broncos could reach 30 points this week. That could make it tough for Mendoza to cover the spread. He's actually the first rookie quarterback to ever face both of the previous season's No. 1 seeds in his first two career starts.  …  Prediction: Broncos 30, Raiders 17

Dubin (Raiders +10): The Broncos have seven wins this year, and six of them are by one score. The only team they beat by more than seven points is the Cardinals. I reserve the right to change this pick if Brock Bowers is out and Fernando Mendoza just doesn't have anyone at all to throw the ball to, but otherwise the Broncos just don't seem like a team capable of blowing out an opponent that has actually played fairly well this year.  … Prediction: Broncos 21, Raiders 17

Dajani (Giants +6): No one is debating that the Jaguars are not one of the best teams in the NFL, but they haven't exactly been tested recently. They blew out the hapless Colts, had no problem with Joe Fagnano's Baltimore Ravens and then dropped 40 points on the one-win Tennessee Titans. The Giants aren't Super Bowl contenders, but this is easily the best team Jacksonville has played in over the past month. I'm not going to take the Giants to win this game straight up, but I am leaning toward the six points. The Giants have an underrated defense that currently ranks No. 5 in the NFL in yards allowed per game (305.7), and J.J. McCarthy has the fifth-most yards per attempt (8.8) since his Giants debut in Week 5. Both of these teams are 6-3 ATS this season. Give me the Giants with a back-door cover.  …  Prediction: Jaguars 23, Giants 18

Dubin (Jaguars -6): Unlike the Broncos, the Jaguars have blown out everybody. Five of their seven wins have come by 17 points or more, including each of their last three games. The Giants are probably better than the Colts, Ravens and Titans, but I don't see them hanging with this Jacksonville offense — not with the Jags getting their new defensive stalwarts on the field for the first time since the trade deadline. (Jessie Bates III and Jordan Davis sat out last week because they had yet to have their bye and the Jags had already taken theirs.) … Prediction: Jaguars 31, Giants 20

Dajani (49ers -3): The 49ers are coming off a ridiculous 46-40 win over the Cowboys, where they recorded the most total yards in a road game in franchise history (584) and averaged a whopping 9.4 yards per play. Brock Purdy's offense had three touchdowns of 65+ yards! Christian McCaffrey actually became the first running back in NFL history to record two 65-yard receiving touchdowns in a game. Obviously, the Vikings' defense is MUCH better than the Cowboys', but something you should know is that this game is in Mexico City. And both teams have prepared for it differently.

The stadium the 49ers and Vikings will play in on Sunday is over 7,000 feet above sea level. So, the 49ers traveled to the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs this week, which is at an elevation of 6,621 feet, to prepare. The Vikings, on the other hand, apparently built an altitude chamber so players can get familiar with "thinner air" before Sunday, but otherwise are seemingly pulling a Los Angeles Rams and just showing up on site the day before the game. The 49ers dominated the Rams in Australia in Week 1, 27-7, and part of that was because their travel plans were so much better. The 49ers have won and covered in four straight International games. …  Prediction: 49ers 26, Vikings 20

Dubin (49ers -3): In a battle of a great offense against a great defense, I am usually going to lean toward the offensive side unless there's a really compelling reason in favor of the defensive-minded team. Kirk Cousins' ability to elevate the Vikings' own offense almost provides that reason, but it's not quite enough for me to get there. This San Francisco offense is too much of a well-oiled machine for me to pick against the Niners — even in a matchup with a defensive coordinator as crazy and as good as Brian Flores.  … Prediction: 49ers 23, Vikings 17

Dajani (Bengals -6.5): Before you think this is some easy pick to make just because of how hot the Bengals are, know that Cincy is 0-2-1 in its past three games against the Washington Commanders, who just upset the Giants in New York last week. Jayden Daniels' coming-out party as a rookie actually came against the Bengals. Still, it's hard to go against my Super Bowl pick and my MVP pick this season.

The Bengals are 6-2 SU and 6-1-1 ATS in their last eight road games and have scored at least 30 points in three straight on the road. Joe Burrow is on pace for the highest completion percentage (74.7%) in a season in NFL history, and he also leads the league in passing yards per game (310.6), passing touchdowns (27) and passer rating (117.7). His MVP case is aided by the dynamic duo of Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, who are on pace to become the first teammate duo to both record 1,500 yards receiving in a season. …  Prediction: Bengals 27, Commanders 20

Dubin (Bengals -6.5): The current version of the Commanders does not have the firepower to keep up with the Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins show. I'm not sure any version of the Commanders ever did, but even after winning two of their last three games, they haven't exactly looked impressive. The Bengals, meanwhile, are putting on an aerial assault for the ages every week. … Prediction: Bengals 31, Commanders 20
